#5576. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5575. Agent demand can’t be forecast, meaning the database has to be ready for anything

Enterprises building an agentic AI architecture are learning that the database matters as much as the model. AI agents fire off thousands of unplanned queries at once — and expect answers in milliseconds.

PhoenixAI, the trade name of CelerData Inc., raised $80 million this year to develop database technology for AI agents to solve this growing problem. Established players struggle to return answers in real time, according to Ross Armstrong (pictured), senior vice president of global sales of PhoenixAI.

“There was a real gap in the market for real-time analytics, and to be able to not only ask a question but get the response back in real time was something that all the database players that are out there, even the big names in the market, couldn’t do well,” Armstrong said. “If you have customer-facing analytics or agentic AI … you need that response time to be able to meet the SLAs with your customers.”

Armstrong spoke with theCUBE’s Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the database demands of agentic AI, real-time query performance and the need for governance and observability. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents generate queries in real time and may hit several databases at once, according to Armstrong. PhoenixAI’s specific columnar engine handles structured and unstructured data and works out how to answer each query as it arrives.

“I think what the biggest demand is that we don’t know what the demand is going to be from those agents,” Armstrong said. “You could have … thousands and thousands of queries hitting at the exact same time, but you still need that real speedy response.”

PhoenixAI joined Cloudera as a foundational database partner and is now an option in Cloudera’s marketplace. Its self-managed edition, PhoenixAI Anywhere, runs in a customer’s cloud, on-premises or in air-gapped environments. In a market where many early adopters hit governance and observability problems, PhoenixAI plans to address them with AgentBase, a purpose-built context environment that keeps agents away from data they don’t need, Armstrong explained.

“You can design that playground for those agents to be protected and to be governed but also to give them access to the data that you need,” Armstrong said. “It’s not necessary to run agents on a solution like PhoenixAI, but it’s certainly one that helps you put those guardrails in that a lot of organizations are looking for.”

#5573. Reju Expands Industry Network Through its Work with Six Mills

Reju is collaborating with A. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Swisstex Direct, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics and Utenos to strengthen Reju's path to industrial-scale, post-consumer textile-to-textile regeneration.

PARIS, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Reju, the textile-to-textile regeneration company, today announced that it has been collaborating with six mills to develop fabrics in order to accelerate the integration of regenerated polyester into the global textile supply chain. The work is being carried out with A. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics and Utenos in Europe and Swisstex Direct in the United States, thereby growing a network for premium knitting, seamless construction, technical wovens, and advanced dyeing and finishing. The ongoing work is designed to move Reju's regenerated polyester further downstream, from raw output at its future Regeneration Hubs into finished fabric.

Together, these six mills bring complementary specializations across the textile value chain:

This gives Reju access to mills spanning circular knit design, chain-of-custody verified recycling, high-volume jersey production, and sustainability-certified dyeing and finishing, the manufacturing capabilities needed to move regenerated polyester from raw material into finished, market-ready fabric at scale.

"Every selected mill with whom we are working adds to our circular textile system," said Patrik Frisk, CEO of Reju. "As plans for Reju's future Regeneration Hub network grows, so will our ability to deliver a consistent, high-quality regenerated polyester that manufacturers and brands can then build on."

Each on-going workstream is tied to specific development projects underway across Reju's manufacturing network, work that reflects real market demand the company is tracking with its growing roster of brand with whom it has signed development agreements.

The mill announcements build on a year of strong momentum for Reju, including: the â¬135 million from NIKI the Dutch government funding to support the facility; the selection of Rochester, New York as its first North American regeneration hub and an additional site selection for a future regeneration hub in Lacq, France.

"By bringing mills like these into our ecosystem, we can turn regenerated material into real product," Frisk added. "It's how we close the loop, not just in theory, but from textile waste to finished fabric."

With access to an expanded manufacturing network, Reju is positioning itself to deliver regenerated polyester at the quality and scale required for mainstream adoption, moving the industry closer to a true textile-to-textile circular system.

Reju is a materials regeneration company focused on creating innovative solutions for regenerating polyester textiles from post-consumer PET waste. Owned by Technip Energies and utilizing technology originating with IBM Research, Reju is driven by its purpose to unlock infinite possibilities within finite resources. The company aims to establish a global textile recycling circular system to regenerate and recirculate polyester textiles. Learn more at https://www.reju.com/.

With over 75 years of experience, we are market leaders in developing and manufacturing circular knitted fabrics.

We have always based our decisions on the values we value most. Dedication to Work, Trust, Transparency, and Social Responsibility combined with our focus on Technology, Innovation, Know-How, Flexibility, and Sustainability. The blend of all these factors distinctively marks the essence of our business model and A. Sampaio's path in the national and international textile industry.

We know how to anticipate customer needs and offer the correct solution, from essential fabrics to developments with increasingly innovative and complex structures and raw materials, crossing all creative boundaries.

At A. Sampaio, we pride ourselves on building relationships based on Trust and Transparency. These relationships underpin our company's and all partners' success in an economy that increasingly wants to be circular. We create value while respecting the ecosystem and everyone's future.

Thriving at the textile frontier, FOV Fabrics fuses advanced textile functionality with circular sustainability. And boasting a fully vertical process, which includes creative design, cutting-edge R&D as well as the latest production technologies, we believe anything is possible.

Swisstex Direct is a provider of circular knit fabrics with locations in Los Angeles and El Salvador, offering knitting, dyeing, finishing, and collaborative product development for apparel brands. With more than 20 years of experience, the company offers a broad range of knit constructions, natural and synthetic fibers, recycled materials, and performance finishes. As a BluesignÂ® system partner, Swisstex Direct combines technical innovation with a commitment to responsible textile production, quality, and responsive customer service. For more information, visit swisstexdirect.com.

TINTEX specializes in crafting circular-knitted fabrics and developing sustainable strategies throughout the entire supply chain.

Based in Vila Nova de Cerveira, Portugal, the company draws on over 25 years of textile experience to create both timeless and contemporary, eco-conscious, and innovative fabrics for the Fashion, Activewear, Loungewear, and Underwear segments.

Utenos Trikotazas, a vertically integrated circular knit fabric and garment manufacturer in the Baltic States, combining over 50 years of textile expertise with European manufacturing excellence and certifications including OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100, GOTS, RWS, GRS, WOOLMARK, SMETA, ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

RDD is a Portuguese textile company developing innovative textiles, from fibres to finished fabrics. Using emerging technologies and novel raw materials, RDD creates sustainable fabrics through a more environmentally friendly production process. Its focus lies in bio-based, regenerative and recycled materials, along with pioneering dyeing technologies that reduce environmental impact, supporting more responsible production and consumption. By bringing together science, design and technology, RDD rethinks how materials are imagined, made and valued.

#5572. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5571. Project-by-project security reviews can’t keep pace with enterprise AI agents

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are finding that tokenization and other data protection methods now decide how fast those projects move.

But sensitive data fed into models is hard to pull back — and security reviews built for a slower era are stalling deployments. The challenge is shifting from locking data down to keeping it usable once it is protected. That tension is playing out across Cloudera Inc.’s partner ecosystem, where security is becoming a prerequisite for AI value rather than a final gate, according to Diego Loureda (pictured), vice president of customer success and presales at Protegrity USA Inc.

“Data leaks are still a thing. If you put sensitive data on a model, if you put sensitive data on a vector store or in the memory of an agent that is going to propagate to other agents, good luck removing that sensitive data,” Loureda said. “There’s no way you’re going to be able to do that.”

Loureda spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed data security along with Protegrity being named Cloudera’s Emerging Technology Partner of the Year. (* Disclosure below.)

Traditional encryption can lock data so tightly that analysts and models can no longer use it. Protegrity centers its approach on tokenization, which swaps sensitive values for substitutes instead of relying on a mathematical algorithm, Loureda explained. That design also matters as quantum computing threatens today’s cryptography.

“Our main method of protection, that is tokenization, it’s already quantum ready,” Loureda said. “The reason behind that is because there is no mathematical algorithm behind it. It’s all based on replacement in memory.”

Protection alone doesn’t solve the speed problem, however. In research Protegrity commissioned from Enterprise Management Associates Inc., 83% of leaders reported project delays, Loureda noted.

“The main problem with governance is that companies are approving projects and that will not scale in the age of AI,” Loureda said. “They have to approve patterns.”

The same study found 82% of leaders push agents into production in a diminished state, stripped of the tools and data that would make them useful, he added. Controls such as tokenization let security teams clear the way for those agents instead, according to Loureda.

“Security has always been the business of no, the department of no. That changes now,” he said. “These days security is the team that can enable AI to give you value.”

#5568. Northern California MLSListings joins Compass antitrust fight

MLSListings joined 6 MLSs in an amended SDNY complaint seeking declaratory relief and an injunction to keep enforcing cooperation rules. The suit cites Compass demand letters and threats of litigation over office exclusive marketing.  AI Summary

Yet another MLS is suing Compass International Holdings.

The amended complaint reiterates the claims made in the initial complaint, which was filed by Arizona Regional MLS, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, Hive MLS, and Doorify MLS.

Through this lawsuit, the MLS plaintiffs are asking the court to allow them to continue enforcing their cooperation rules and policies without violating antitrust law, as well as an injunction permanently barring Compass from “bringing or pursuing any claim against any MLS Party alleging that the Cooperation Rules violate the federal antitrust laws or the state antitrust laws.”

As in the initial complaint, the MLSs claim they were prompted to file this lawsuit after Compass sent demand letters to MLSs across the country in early September, threatening to sue them if they did not stop fining or penalizing Compass’s agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin reiterated these threats on stage at the Council of MLSs’ Open House conference in late September, claiming that his firm would spend millions of dollars pursuing litigation against MLSs that refused to comply.

While Compass has contended in public statements and in its recently filed lawsuit against CRMLS, that the MLS is anticompetitive as it is made up of a board of competitors that are creating rules governing how Compass and other members can run their businesses, the six MLS plaintiffs argue that their cooperation rules promote competition among broker members.

In addition, the MLSs contend that the rules help prevent brokers from using the MLS to find buyers while withholding their own listings from free-riding on the contributions of other participants. The complaint also cites the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice‘s 2007 report on competition in real estate brokerage to support its position that MLSs create efficiencies and provide meaningful benefits to consumers.

In an emailed statement, a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that “it’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true.”

“For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?” the spokesperson added. “An agent’s fiduciary duty is to their client, not to the MLS. Only the law and the homeowner should tell real estate professionals how to publicly market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner.”

The claims in this lawsuit are nearly identical to those made in a lawsuit filed earlier in October by California Regional MLS (CRMLS) also in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Last week, the New York-based OneKey MLS joined CRMLSs lawsuit against Compass.

For its part, Compass has filed its own lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging that the MLS’s rules unlawfully restrict how homeowners and their agents can publicly market properties outside the MLS. The firm has yet to file a lawsuit against another MLS, despite its lingering threats.

#5567. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5565. Before the price cut: A first-week real estate listing review

A first-week listing review should start with exposure and showing access, then separate activity from feedback. Next, compare competing actives and recent sales to diagnose friction before recommending a single next action.  AI Summary

An early listing review is a decision point, not an automatic countdown to a price reduction. The useful question is not simply whether a home has received attention. It is where the process may be losing buyers: before they see the property, when they try to access it or after they compare it with other options.

A three-part review helps keep those questions separate. First, verify exposure and access. Then read activity and feedback as different kinds of evidence. Finally, compare the home with the alternatives buyers can choose now and the properties that have recently sold. The order matters. There is little value in interpreting a quiet showing calendar before confirming that the listing is being presented accurately and can be toured as intended.

Start with the mechanics. Confirm that the status, price, address, remarks, photos, floor plan, if provided, and showing instructions are correct wherever the listing appears. Check that the media loads, links work and the showing process is clear.

Review the calendar for declined, canceled or difficult-to-schedule requests, and ask whether access constraints are limiting the available appointment windows. These checks do not prove that exposure is the problem. They establish whether the marketing and access buyers are encountering match the plan.

Activity includes inquiries, showing requests, completed tours, repeat visits and offers. Feedback is what a buyer or agent says about the home. The two are related, but they answer different questions. A home may have few tours and little feedback, which gives an agent limited evidence about buyer reaction inside the property. Another may draw tours but receive recurring comments about the same feature. Those are different situations and call for different investigations.

Keep the record specific. Note the date and type of each inquiry or tour, whether it was completed, and any follow-up that is still outstanding. Record feedback in the speaker’s terms, then distinguish direct observations from interpretation. A comment that a kitchen feels dated is a specific reaction.

A conclusion that buyers consider the home overpriced is broader and should be tested against other evidence, not inferred from one comment. A single reaction can be useful, but it is not a pattern.

Review current competing listings that a buyer could reasonably consider alongside the home. Compare meaningful points such as location, condition, layout, updates, presentation and terms, rather than just matching bedroom and bathroom counts.

Then, review recent closed sales to understand what buyers have actually purchased in the relevant area and property segment. Active listings show the choices in front of buyers; closed sales provide a separate reference point. Neither list is a substitute for judgment about how closely each property matches.

Look for repeated signals across these sources. If several unrelated buyers mention the same condition issue, and competing homes present that feature differently, the feedback deserves attention. If tours are limited while the listing has a correct presentation but competes against homes that appear to offer more for similar terms, price may be part of the diagnosis.

If activity is constrained by scheduling or incomplete exposure, correct those issues without overlooking evidence that the price also needs attention. These are working hypotheses, not formulas. The pace and meaning of early activity vary by property and market, so no fixed number of days or showings can answer the question in every case.

Set the review date with the seller when the listing launches. Agree on what information will be reviewed, how feedback will be gathered, and what kind of change would warrant a conversation. A first-week checkpoint can be useful, but it is not a universal deadline for a decision. The timing should reflect the listing’s circumstances and the amount of meaningful evidence available.

At that conversation, organize the findings into three possible sources of friction: price, exposure or access, and how the home compares with buyers’ needs and alternatives. Then recommend one principal next action. That may be correcting a listing detail or access issue, improving a specific part of the presentation, or making no change while a defined piece of evidence is gathered.

If the comparison and repeated response support a price adjustment, explain the evidence and recommend a deliberate repositioning that reflects the alternatives buyers are seeing. A reduction should be tied to that diagnosis, not used as a reflexive response to one soft metric.

A disciplined review gives the seller a clearer basis for deciding what to do next. It also gives the agent a practical way to be candid without overreading limited feedback or delaying a justified change. The aim is not to defend the original list price or to reduce it by default. It is to identify the most likely point of friction, show the evidence behind that view, and make the next move count.

Andrew Piane is an Arizona Realtor with HomeSmart and has eight years of experience in residential real estate.

#5564. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5563. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5561. eLEND expands credit eligibility for FHA cash-out refis, conventional loans

eLEND launched CreditEdge, expanding eligibility for FHA cash-out refinances to 500 credit scores and conventional loans below 620, subject to AUS approval. Loans on primary residences must be locked by Dec. 31, 2026, across retail, wholesale and nondelegated correspondent channels.   AI Summary

New Jersey-based mortgage lender eLEND is expanding credit score eligibility for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) cash-out refinances and conventional loans through a limited-time incentive designed to give borrowers with lower credit scores more financing options.

The program, called CreditEdge, allows FHA cash-out refinance borrowers to qualify with credit scores as low as 500 and conventional borrowers to qualify with scores below 620, subject to approval through automated underwriting systems (AUS).

The expanded guidelines apply to primary residences and are available through eLEND’s retail, wholesale and nondelegated correspondent channels. Loans must be locked by Dec. 31, 2026, to qualify.

“The Fed held rates steady last week, and with inflation still weighing on the economy, affordability can’t wait on rate relief,” said Rob Pieklo, president and CEO of eLEND. “That’s why we’re focused on what we can control. Expanding credit score requirements, backed by AUS approval to evaluate each borrower’s ability to repay, gives our broker partners more ways to get deals done and helps more people get into homes.”

For FHA cash-out refinances, the minimum credit score is 500. Fannie Mae- and Freddie Mac-backed conventional loans are eligible with scores below 620, although a minimum score of 600 applies when private mortgage insurance is required.

All loans must receive an Approve/Eligible finding from Fannie Mae’s Desktop Underwriter or an Accept finding from Freddie Mac’s Loan Product Advisor.

“Our broker partners tell us credit score requirements are one of the main reasons they have to turn borrowers away,” said Michael Brenning, chief operating officer of eLEND. “That’s changing. With expanded credit score requirements on FHA cash-outs and conventional loans, our partners can help clients tap into their equity, get more first-time homebuyers in the door, and close more loans before year-end. And with every loan backed by AUS approval, we’re expanding access without compromising on responsible lending.”

eLEND said the program pairs expanded credit score requirements with automated underwriting to maintain its lending standards. AUS evaluates a borrower’s broader financial profile, including income, assets, debts and payment history, rather than relying solely on a credit score.

CreditEdge is part of a broader effort by eLEND to expand its product offerings for mortgage brokers and lending partners. Recent additions include an expanded renovation lending suite featuring the AI-powered Ready4Remodel platform, eXPRESS HELOC and debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) loans. The company also said jumbo AUS is coming soon.

American Financial Resources, which rebranded to eLEND last year, has produced a year-to-date volume of $405.7 million, according to RETR data.

#5560. With Agentic Studio, LinearB provides the critical context needed to accelerate software delivery

Application development intelligence startup LinearB Inc. said today it’s trying to ease the growing congestion in organization’s software delivery pipelines that has arisen with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence coding tools.

It’s doing so with Agentic Studio, a new offering announced today that’s focused on providing more actionable context for human engineers and autonomous coding agents alike.

The startup says the emergence of generative AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex has led to new headaches for enterprise software development teams. Though writing software code now can be basically effortless, shipping that code into production is still as painful as it has always been, and now they have much more of it to ship.

In its recent Software Engineering Benchmarks report, the company analyzed more than 2.7 million pull requests across 250 organizations and found that those who rely on AI coding tools have almost doubled their merged code changes year-over-year. But the problem is that AI-assisted pull requests are nearly 2.6 times larger, and consequently they’re waiting more than five times longer to be reviewed.

That has led to significant backlogs. And it’s compounded by the fact that AI agent’s proposed code changes are merged just 79% of the time at “elite organizations,” compared with 92% for human-authored code.

LinearB says that human software engineers struggle to clear this backlog because the traditional dashboards they’re forced to work with only provide metrics, rather than the context needed to resolve those pull requests. With Agentic Studio, it’s trying to address this by normalizing the data and insights generated by Git repositories and project tracking tools into a unified context layer. It means that instead of muddling through various charts to try and understand why release velocity has stalled, software engineers can ask questions in plain language to understand the root cause and receive recommendations on how to speed things up.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Ori Keren said context has become the new king, not only for AI tools but also for humans. “We realized we hold a knowledge graph that nobody else has of everything that is happening across the software delivery lifecycle,” he said. “That’s exactly what agents and teams need to deliver high quality software faster, so we rebuilt LinearB around it.”

What’s different about Agentic Studio is that it’s designed to help autonomous coding agents just as much as human software engineers, Keren said. By integrating through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, it feeds historical context such as rework rates, past production incidents and code ownership to AI agents, preventing them from making blind modifications to pull requests.

Early adopters have benefited from dramatically increased productivity with Agentic Studio. A case in point is the cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, which used LinearB’s MCP integration to pinpoint why its code reviews were lagging. It discovered that timezone misalignments were the main culprit rather than pull request sizes, and subsequently reorganized its workflows to cut its review times by more than half within just four months.

“For years, engineering leaders told us the same thing: metrics are useful, but they don’t tell you what to do,” said LinearB’s chief operating officer Dan Lines. “A dashboard says your cycle time is two days, but so what? Now [with Agentic Studio] a leader can ask what to improve in their engineering organization and get a clear answer. When that same context goes to coding agents, the platform is not just reporting, it’s acting.”

To help AI agents operationalize the context it provides, LinearB is developing a bunch of new agent skills. The first one, an “effort skill,” is available in early access now and analyzes the complexity of a pull request and its proposed code changes, its rework history and risk to calibrate dynamically how much computational effort a coding agent needs to expend as it works on it.

Simple, low-risk changes are done faster with minimal tokens. More sensitive, high-priority modifications will be implemented with deeper reasoning and more exhaustive testing to ensure nothing goes wrong.

LinearB said it’s planning to expand its agent skills library in the coming months with additional skills focused on automated code review, merge governance and token cost optimization.

#5559. Windward Expands into Maritime Visual Intelligence with Acquisition of Azimut.ai

The newly added sensing layer identifies and fingerprints vessels in real time at maritime chokepoints and ports, enabling the visibility of vessels even when they go dark to evade detection

LONDON and WASHINGTON, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Windward, the leading Maritime AIâ¢ company, today announced the acquisition of Azimut.ai, a maritime visual intelligence company. The acquisition adds an optical sensing layer to Windward's multi-source platform and marks the company's first step into ground and ship-based sensors that provide additional visibility into an opaque maritime environment.

Today's maritime operational picture is more robust than it has ever been, relying on a rich mix of sources, including AIS, satellite imagery, and RF, that each deliver tremendous value. "Together, as a community, we are stronger. We invite all stakeholders in the maritime domain, as well as anyone who wants to make a difference for safer and more secure oceans, to reach out and become a site partner."

The acquisition reflects the three layers on which Windward's platform stands. At the base, vast multi-source datasets feed into one all-source operational and intelligence picture. Layered on top of that is Windward's Maritime AI, the behavioral pattern recognition, vessel verification, and anomaly detection that turn raw inputs into actionable findings. The final layer is partnership. Windward designs each capability around the operational needs of its customers, so it can provide technology to support every mission.

Windward is the leading Maritime AIâ¢ company, delivering mission-grade, multi-source intelligence for all maritime-based operations. #5558. Best real estate continuing education schools for license renewal in 2026

Our editors independently review the products we recommend. When you buy through our links, we may earn a commission. Learn more

Is your license renewal on the horizon? Maintaining your real estate license means taking continuing education courses to fulfill your state licensing board’s requirements, and doing so before your license expires.

You can complete your real estate CE hours online through one of the many course providers that offer state-specific packages and electives. But it can be challenging to narrow down the best real estate school for you. That’s why we’re sharing our top four online real estate continuing education providers, highlighting the states in which they offer courses and our favorite features.

Colibri offers real estate CE courses in all 50 states and Washington, D.C., with customized online bundles available. Complete your state’s required CE courses on your own time, at your own pace. More than 500,000 agents have completed Colibri Real Estate’s courses. Colibri offers a satisfaction guarantee and refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for self-paced online courses.

When it comes to course format and content delivery, choose from Colibri’s self-paced online and instructor-led livestream courses, which are designed to allow you to study on any device with internet access and a browser. That means you can meet all of your state requirements using your smartphone or tablet. Course content is written and taught by active, seasoned industry professionals, and course upgrades feature engagement with instructors experienced in your local market.

Our favorite feature is the intuitive, online platform and dashboard, which you can access 24/7. With Colibri’s online courses, you can stop and start up again anytime, without losing track of your progress.

Colibri’s real estate continuing education course offerings vary by state, but a sampling of intriguing topics we researched includes Fair Housing, ethics, handling multiple offers, educating buyers, handling trust funds and implicit bias training. Some states require core courses while others let agents choose from a series of electives, so click the button above to visit Colibri and choose your state from their drop-down menu.

Depending on your state, post-licensing packages start as low as $109 and up to $279, with individual courses ranging from $29 to $54. And CE renewal packages start as low as $89 and up to $189, with individual courses ranging from $22 to $49.

The CE Shop offers real estate continuing education courses in all 50 states, plus Washington D.C., and allows students to choose from full packages that include all post-licensing hours needed for first-time license renewal. Or get your mandatory education hours by taking individual post-licensing courses. While course expiration dates vary by state, they are generally one year after the date of purchase.

The CE Shop is our pick for the best value in real estate continuing education because of all the options it affords agents renewing their license. If you’re licensed in multiple states, the CE Shop spares you from purchasing multiple packages and repeating reciprocal courses by creating multistate and custom packages tailored to your needs and budget. Students also have exclusive access to Agent Perks, a program that includes special discounts, offers, and trials from the CE Shop’s partners to help you better automate your real practice.

The CE Shop’s course format and content delivery are also noteworthy, as courses can be accessed through your tablet, computer, or smartphone 24/7.

The CE Shop’s real estate continuing education topics may include tax-deferred exchanges, real estate finance, USDA rural loans or real estate advertising compliance. Course offerings and bundles vary by state and according to state requirements. In many states, the CE Shop’s continuing education courses can be bundled with their prelicensing courses, offering convenience and significant savings.

Depending on your state, post-licensing CE packages start as low as $105 and up to $609, with individual courses ranging from $9 to $265 for first-time renewals. Subsequent renewal course packages start as low as $39 and up to $249, with individual courses ranging from $9 to $115.

Check out this e-book from The CE Shop that goes through the salary, skills, benefits and education needed to become a successful home inspector.

Aceable Agent offers continuing education courses to renew your license in Georgia, Texas, and Florida. Their courses are created by active industry experts in collaboration with Harvard-educated instructional designers. After you complete your final course test, Aceable Agent will process your Certificate of Completion to ensure that you get credit for completing your CE course with your state licensing board.

As far as course format and content delivery, Aceable Agent’s students can access self-paced, online courses on their computer, laptop, tablet, or smartphone. Interactive continuing education courses feature real-world scenarios to keep you engaged. Course content is delivered in bite-sized pieces, making it easier to retain the course’s information. Choose from a selection of individual courses or a course bundle for convenience and savings.

Our favorite feature is Aceable Agent’s mobile app. Aceable Agent was the first online real estate school to offer courses through a mobile app. Students can even switch between their browser and Aceable Agent’s mobile app, both of which track progress and save it — so you can stop and resume your studies on multiple devices. You can even tune into audio lessons as you’d listen to your favorite podcast.

Aceable Agent’s real estate continuing education course offerings vary by state and state CE requirements. For example, Texas agents can choose from the Legal Update Bundle (just the mandatory courses) or the 18-hour Bundle (mandatory courses plus electives). New York agents can quickly complete the NYREC-approved, 22.5-hour, all-in-one package. Georgia agents opting for Aceable Agent will take courses through a partnership with Kaplan Real Estate Education. Click the button above to learn more.

Depending on your state, continuing education bundles start as low as $135 and up to $469, with some individual courses starting at $30. Full course refunds are available within 30 days of purchase, as long as you have not completed the course.

Kaplan offers CE courses in all 50 states and post-licensing courses for first-time renewals in the following states: Alabama, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Mississippi, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

A convenient online format allows students to access courses easily through a tablet or mobile device. And Kaplan’s online system connects you to courses designed to fit your learning style and build your education around your schedule. Although Kaplan’s CE packages aren’t as affordable as other schools, the cost may be worth it to students who need self-paced, interactive online content.

Our favorite course feature is the option to upgrade. Kaplan offers state-approved CE courses to help you complete the required hours of approved education, and you can take one CE class as a stand-alone online course for a lower price point or upgrade to a complete CE package. And behind the school’s continuing education courses is a staff that will help you not only navigate your course but also stay on top of industry trends.

Product offerings include continuing education courses, prelicensing courses, and exam prep in many states. Boasting over 50 years of experience, Kaplan has helped thousands of students begin and advance their real estate careers each year.

Depending on your state, post-licensing CE packages for first-time renewals start as low as $299 and up to $799, with individual courses ranging from $165 to $259. And CE renewal packages start as low as $69 and up to $229, with individual courses ranging from $19 to $69. Full tuition refunds are available within 30 days of purchase for web-based courses and online classes that have not been completed.

McKissock Learning offers a wide range of real estate CE courses, covering both required and elective subjects. You’ll find courses on fair housing, ethics and license law alongside more specialized topics like property management, real estate investing and buyer and seller representation. The catalog also covers newer areas such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence in real estate, giving agents more flexibility in choosing what they want to learn beyond their required credits.

Beyond its CE catalog, McKissock offers additional resources through its Learning Snacks library. These include shorter, practical materials such as templates, checklists and white papers that agents can use in their day-to-day work.

Higher-tier plans offer additional learning opportunities, including AI MasterTracks, complimentary professional certifications and discounts on other programs. And if you’re licensed in multiple states, you can opt for a multi-state plan to access eligible CE courses across states under one membership.

Single-state memberships start at $35, though pricing varies by state. Multi-state plans range from $329 to $439 per year. If you don’t need an annual membership, you can purchase individual CE courses instead and choose the ones that best fit your interests and requirements.

To determine the very best online real estate schools for continuing education, we’ve evaluated national and state-specific online real estate education providers. Across dozens of articles, we’ve gained in-depth knowledge of real estate online post-licensing and continuing education courses, analyzing each school based on course offerings, study tools, format options and flexibility, accessibility, student support services, user reviews, and affordability.

Equipped with this depth of knowledge, we narrowed this list down to the top four real estate schools nationwide for convenience, excellence in course content, flexibility, value, and user experience. Providing economies of scale, these schools’ course packages are more affordable thanks to technology that makes their online courses way more convenient than having to commute to a local state school to attend in-person classes. Unlike your local school, these industry-leading schools have the scale to invest in helpful technology that makes renewing your state license a breeze, so you can get back to working with your clients and advancing your career.

You’re responsible for helping clients navigate one of the most important financial decisions of their lives. That’s why you must stay up to speed on the latest information, from real estate law and contracts to environmental issues like climate change.

Not only is it required that you renew your license to stay current, but it’s also beneficial to maintain your skills and expand your industry knowledge through formal education.

Real estate continuing education requirements to maintain your real estate license vary from state to state, but most require that you take a set number of hours of CE course hours every two years.

Some states, like West Virginia, require as few as seven CE hours, while states like Texas require 270 qualifying course hours.

Keep in mind that prices vary greatly from state to state, and each school in this buyer’s guide offers budget-friendly course options.

For the purposes of this real estate school guide, we priced out four of the industry-leading schools, based on their offerings in different areas of the country, to determine an average cost of $539 for CE packages and $20 for individual CE courses.
