#5557. Exclusive: Guardz brings Palo Alto Networks browser protection to MSPs serving small businesses

Cybersecurity startup Guardz Cyber Ltd. today added browser protection from Palo Alto Networks Inc.’s Prisma Browser for Business to its security platform for managed service providers that protect small businesses.

The integration is aimed at phishing attacks that slip between separate security tools. A typical one starts with an email that lures an employee to a counterfeit login page, and the credentials typed there can put connected accounts at risk. “For most small businesses, the browser is now the office,” said Shivam Srivastava, vice president of product at Palo Alto Networks.

Prisma Browser for Business can block the page when the link is clicked. Guardz then matches that browser event to the original email, related Microsoft 365 activity and endpoint telemetry for the same user identity. From there, the provider and Guardz’s 24/7 managed detection and response team can work the whole chain as a single incident.

The browser-side detection comes from Palo Alto Networks. Inline machine-learning models screen pages for phishing, and Advanced URL Filtering helps block malicious sites, including fake sign-in pages and attacks built to steal live session tokens. The company’s WildFire service analyzes suspect files. Uploads and downloads are scanned as they pass through the browser, which also picks out risky extensions.

Guardz Co-founder and Chief Executive Dor Eisner called the browser “the primary gateway to the modern workspace.” Traditional security tools work in silos that leave gaps in visibility and response, he said, and the agents running on Guardz’s platform are meant to let providers investigate threats autonomously anywhere in that workspace.

Setup falls to Guardz, which handles provisioning and default configuration. Kevin Kehoe of early-access provider Datawise Networks Inc. said the rollout through his firm’s remote monitoring and management software was “super smooth.” Within minutes, he said, the browser extension was “on every Chrome and Edge profile.”

For generative artificial intelligence services used in the browser, Guardz’s AI Usage and Control features let technicians set a separate policy for each client. Those policies can restrict copying, pasting and file transfers by website or by category. Guardz has also introduced a report that gives providers a per-client view of AI tool usage.

Palo Alto Networks moved into enterprise browsers with its 2023 acquisition of Israeli startup Talon Cyber Security Ltd. Prisma Browser for Business, its version for small businesses, went on sale in the U.S. in March.

Guardz is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $84 million, including a $56 million Series B round led by ClearSky in June 2025.

#5554. MazeBolt launches native RADAR deployment for Akamai DDoS protection customers

Distributed denial-of-service testing company MazeBolt Technologies Ltd. today launched a native deployment of its RADAR validation platform for customers of Akamai Technologies Inc.

Enterprises using Akamai’s DDoS protection can have continuous testing running within hours without taking services offline. The release targets the configuration gaps that open up as a company adds services, application programming interfaces and regions behind its DDoS protection.

Akamai setups are rarely tested independently against each of those changes, according to MazeBolt, and a gap can stay hidden until an attack reaches a login page or a payment flow. Founder and Chief Executive Matthew Andriani said testing “even a few times a year cannot keep pace” now that artificial intelligence projects keep adding new services and APIs.

Akamai’s own State of the Internet report, published in March, found that Layer 7 DDoS attacks rose 104% over two years, and the company blamed part of that growth on attack tools that use AI to make web applications and APIs easier to hit.

RADAR fires simulated attacks at Akamai-protected services from inside the customer’s own environment. The attack library covers known vectors as well as the AI-orchestrated and AI-generated attacks MazeBolt added with its VectorAI module in June. When RADAR first tests a production environment, about 37% of attack vectors get past the protection already in place, based on MazeBolt’s data from initial deployments.

Each run ends in a report with remediation guidance written for the specific protection vendor, and RADAR repeats the test once a fix is in place. “Deployed protection is not proven protection,” said Eyal Rahimi, vice president of engineering at MazeBolt. Customers also need to be able to prove which gaps they have closed, Rahimi said.

Most financial institutions test far less often. In a MazeBolt survey of 300 of their security leaders last year, 86% said they test their DDoS defenses once a year or less. Akamai reported in May that the median duration of Layers 3 and 4 DDoS attacks on the sector has risen 738% since 2024.

John Grady, chief analyst at Omdia, said misconfigurations and out-of-date rules remain the source of many security incidents. “DDoS is no different,” Grady said. “It is a critical area where security teams must ensure protection is current, because successful attacks impact availability and directly affect the bottom line.”

Native Layer 7 support for Akamai environments is available today to all RADAR customers. Cloudflare Inc., F5 Inc. and Radware Ltd. are among the other mitigation vendors whose products RADAR already tests across scrubbing centers, on-premises equipment and cloud services.

#5553. Binance Hack: Are Funds Safu? What We Know So Far About the Biggest Heist in Crypto History

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Cryptocurrency giant Binance faces what could be the largest exchange hack in history after a security breach affected an estimated $6.3 billion in digital assets, eclipsing the record-setting $1.5Bn Bybit exploit in 2025. The Binance hack has led the exchange to pledge to cover all losses, while investigators work to identify the attackers and recover the stolen funds.

Binance confirmed that the incident affected approximately $6.3Bn in digital assets, with around $3Bn reportedly frozen on-chain through coordination with blockchain partners and other platforms. However, a substantial portion of the funds may remain under the attackers’ control.

In a statement, Binance co-CEO Richard Teng reassured customers that their funds were safe and that the company would absorb the financial impact using its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and corporate reserves. Former CEO CZ also spoke on the incident, saying on X, “User funds are safe..I don’t manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”

The exchange also temporarily suspended withdrawals while undertaking a security overhaul of its withdrawal infrastructure and associated addresses. Deposits, however, remain unaffected and operational.

Our teams are aware of reports regarding a potential security issue and are actively investigating.I want to be direct: user funds remain SAFE. Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency.🧵

Binance’s preliminary investigation indicates the attack may have originated from a DevOps engineer’s compromised laptop. This breach may have allowed attackers to access a service container, which they used to submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

However, Teng cautioned against viewing this incident as merely a case of stolen employee credentials. He noted that the attacker did not exploit just one engineer’s permissions or carry out a single action.

Instead, he described the incident as a more sophisticated, multi-stage attack. Binance has also emphasized that it has no evidence that any wallet private keys were exposed.

The exchange has revoked authorizations for affected addresses and engaged law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence specialists to trace transactions and recover assets.

Binance plans to publish a detailed technical post-mortem once it completes its investigation, along with an updated Proof of Reserves following the security remediation process.

The identity of those responsible for the Binance hack remains uncertain, although two prominent cryptocurrency analytics firms have independently linked the incident to North Korean cybercriminals.

Both TRM Labs and Chainalysis have pointed to a North Korean hacking operation known as TraderTraitor. Chainalysis reportedly expressed high confidence in the group’s involvement, while TRM Labs identified similarities between the Binance incident and previous attacks attributed to North Korean-linked hackers.

On-chain sleuth ZachXBT also claims that TraderTraitor is responsible, linking wallet addresses from the Binance hack to those from the $388M Bitget exploit earlier this month.

Zach adds that after the Arbitrum Security Council froze $30M in stolen funds, the total amount frozen from the $6.3Bn hack sits at $2.83Bn. Tether, Circle, and Ripple account for most of it.

Binance has not confirmed these allegations and says it is working with law enforcement to identify the perpetrators. The suspected involvement of North Korean hackers is particularly significant given the country’s history of targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset platforms to generate funds.

The most recent major example was the February 2025 attack on Bybit, when hackers believed to be operating under the Lazarus Group stole about $1.5Bn in digital assets.

Within roughly two weeks, the attackers had converted at least $300M into unrecoverable funds. By August 2026, Bybit co-founder and CEO Ben Zhou said the exchange had recovered approximately $48.4M, with another $30.5M frozen.

Update: This brings the total frozen for the Binance exploit so far to over $2.83B pic.twitter.com/AX3utCiIPF

As ZachXBT documented, the scale of the Binance incident has prompted action across the wider cryptocurrency industry. Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle have reportedly frozen about $2.83Bn in assets to prevent further movement of potentially compromised funds.

These interventions highlight the importance of centralized stablecoin issuers and blockchain analytics firms in responding to major cryptocurrency security incidents, particularly when stolen assets move across multiple networks and platforms.

Bitcoin also came under pressure following news of the breach, falling by more than 4% as markets reacted to the security concerns. It remains unclear whether the incident will have a lasting impact on investor confidence or broader cryptocurrency market sentiment.

Founded in 2017, Binance has grown into the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, serving hundreds of millions of registered users globally. Its platform offers spot trading, derivatives, digital wallets, savings products, and other financial services.

The company has faced significant regulatory scrutiny, including the 2023 resignation of founder Changpeng Zhao after he pleaded guilty to money laundering violations in the United States.

Despite the latest incident, Binance insists customer funds remain protected and has committed to absorbing the financial losses.

The immediate priority is to recover as much of the affected cryptocurrency as possible, identify those responsible, and ensure the exchange’s infrastructure is secure before resuming normal withdrawal services.

With the estimated impact potentially exceeding any previous cryptocurrency exchange hack, the incident tests Binance’s security systems, crisis management, and ability to maintain customer confidence.

While this hack could be seen as a true black swan event for the markets, with over $6Bn in funds stolen from the world’s largest crypto exchange, the quick freeze of nearly $3Bn and Binance’s proactive response to the exploit, coupled with its leaders assuring investors that user funds are safe, the market is holding up incredibly well.

Bitcoin briefly fell to $76,500 as news of the Binance hack broke, but has already recovered to over $78,000, absorbing the sell-off with almost no effort. BNB, with its close ties to the exchange, has suffered more, dropping over -6% but is still holding above its longstanding $700 support zone.

Away from coins in the red, several tokens haven’t even flinched at the news and are up over the past 24 hours. Tron is one example: it is up +2% on the day, even though $234M worth of TRX was stolen in the hack.

Hyperliquid seems immune to bad news right now, continuing its recent rally with a +12% daily move as it climbed back above $90 earlier today and looks set to retest its $97 all-time high.

If the hack is brought under control and more funds remain frozen, expect Binance to reimburse users for any lost funds and absorb its own losses with little difficulty. If this happens, the worst is likely over for the crypto market, and it would highlight incredible strength heading into the year-end.

#5551. Could Social Security turmoil influence senior homeowners and reverse mortgage demand?

A 13% surge in early Social Security retirement claims in 2024–2025, driven by political and administrative turmoil at the agency, temporarily reversed a long-term trend of Americans claiming later. Early filing locks in permanently lower benefits, cutting annual income by thousands of dollars for some retirees. Although claim volumes have since normalized, ongoing uncertainty about Social Security’s 2032 funding cliff is pushing some near-retirees to claim sooner.  AI Summary

A sharp but temporary spike in early Social Security claims in 2024 and 2025 underscores a potential trend for the housing market — a greater number of older Americans who are locking in permanently lower retirement income in response to political and administrative uncertainty.

Over the weekend, The New York Times followed up on a report shared last year by HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD). The initial report from the Times found that from October 2024 to April 2025, retirement claims jumped by 267,000, or 13%, compared with the prior year.

Historically, year-over-year fluctuations have been closer to 2% to 3%. Analysts at the Urban Institute and the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College tied the spike to highly publicized turmoil at the Social Security Administration — including staff cuts, office-closure threats and political rhetoric questioning the program’s solvency.

Social Security claims made before the full retirement age (which is now 67 for those born in 1960 or later) permanently reduces monthly benefits. This week, the Times interviewed two claimants — one who gave up about $5,000 a year by filing at 64 and another who sacrificed about $300 a month by filing more than a year early.

These kinds of benefit cuts compound over time and can directly affect housing affordability, especially for owners or renters whose largest fixed expense is their mortgage or rent payment.

As it relates to housing professionals, including reverse mortgage professionals, lower guaranteed income in retirement can translate into a higher likelihood of mortgage payment stress or default among senior homeowners. It can also propel demand for downsizing, shared housing options or migration to lower-cost markets as retirees adjust to tighter budgets.

Additionally, it can mean increased interest for traditional reverse mortgages and similar home equity release products to backfill income gaps. Borrowers in their late 50s and early 60s may be ideally positioned for these products since Social Security filing decisions are imminent, and because seniors are denied for credit at higher rates than the general population.

From October 2025 to April 2026, new claims fell by 235,000, or 10%, essentially offsetting the prior-year surge. But the reporting shows how headlines about Social Security’s finances can directly change claimants’ behavior.

A Boston College experiment cited by the Times this week found that more alarmist headlines led people to say they would claim about a year earlier than those who saw neutral language — regardless of any changes to the underlying facts.

Without congressional action, Social Security’s retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted by late 2032, triggering an automatic benefit cut of up to 22% under current law. The ongoing uncertainty has made Americans in retirement and near retirement “anxious and unhappy,” according to a source who spoke to the Times. This can impact retirement timing, where they choose to live and how much home they can afford.

Multiple policy ideas are circulating on the Social Security front — including bipartisan proposals to lift or eliminate the current $184,500 cap on wages subject to payroll tax, which could inject about $3 trillion into the system over 10 years. But for now, reverse mortgage companies and other housing stakeholders should pay close attention to how Social Security claiming decisions interact with mortgage terms, home equity levels and long-term retirement planning.

In this week’s Monday Morning Q&A, Larissa Morrell of Longbridge Financial told RMD that the demographics of the typical borrower have shifted during her 20-plus years in the industry.

“Historically, a reverse mortgage was really something for people of the older retiree demographic — late 70s, 80s, 90s. Now we do not have that same demographic. Now we’re looking at people of a younger generation. They’re still working. They might be using a reverse mortgage to pay off credit card debt or cover increasing expenses,” Morrell said.

Federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages and proprietary reverse mortgages could allow a borrower to delay Social Security claims by generating additional cash flow or eliminating monthly mortgage payments.

The Social Security Administration notes that people who begin receiving benefits at the full retirement age of 67 get 100% of the monthly benefit. But that percentage increases for every month payments are delayed and can reach up to 124% if a recipients waits until age 70 to make a claim.

But the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has also previously reported that the costs of a reverse mortgage generally exceed the additional increase in benefits that a senior would get by delaying claims.

#5550. AI optimism meets data center backlash as protesters disrupt Seattle AI Week kickoff

by Todd Bishop on Oct 26, 2026 at 10:44 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 11:21 am

The Washington Technology Industry Association kicked off the third annual Seattle AI Week on Monday with a reminder that AI affects everyone, from engineers and artists to “someone who learned about ChatGPT today,” as WTIA’s Nick Ellingson put it.

“All of us should be a part of that conversation,” he added.

A few people in the audience took that statement literally.

Members of Troublemakers, a Seattle climate activism group, interrupted the week’s opening panel on AI and economic growth several times before they were led out by security. Outside on Elliott Bay, others floated in kayaks with a banner: “Power for People, Not for Tech.”

“These are not your constituents — we are,” one protester told Beau Perschbacher, Gov. Bob Ferguson’s senior policy advisor, as he addressed the large crowd of tech and startup leaders at Seattle’s AI House. Perschbacher was on a panel with Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Mattie Zazueta of OpenAI, the event’s presenting sponsor.

The group’s main message, according to members who spoke with GeekWire: the rush to build data centers and roll out AI is putting the state’s communities, jobs and environment at risk, and Washington should be investing in green jobs and clean energy instead.

The protest comes amid a broader backlash against data centers in Washington state and across the country. The Seattle City Council voted unanimously in June to pause new large data centers in the city for a year, and Washington AI Resistance organized at least 19 protests around the state this month calling for a statewide moratorium.

The event also came the same day Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as it spends tens of billions of dollars on data centers and AI infrastructure.

The backlash contrasts with a push from the business and tech community for Washington state and the Seattle region to do more to stay competitive in the AI era.

“Washington helped build the technology economy of the last generation. We have an extraordinary opportunity to lead the AI economy of the next,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, now CEO of the business group Challenge Seattle, in her opening remarks at the AI Week event.

Gregoire cited efforts to put AI to work on the region’s own problems, including an AI permitting pilot in Everett that she said could cut the median wait for an accessory dwelling unit permit from 252 days to 90. She highlighted the AI-driven protein design work of Nobel laureate David Baker of the University of Washington, with applications in areas including the environment, agriculture and health care.

She also warned that Washington is close to the bottom for its business climate, even though it ranks second in North America for tech talent, as other states court its companies and jobs.

On the panel, Perschbacher said Ferguson’s administration has been focused on data centers since taking office, setting up a work group early last year to study their impact. The group looked for a Washington community that had been harmed by a data center and couldn’t find one, he said.

He added that the state won’t permit data centers to run diesel generators around the clock, and that their water use turned out to be “not out of line with a typical industrial user.”

Electricity is a different story. Data centers “use a really significant amount of electricity,” he said, and with demand also rising from EVs and heat pumps, getting enough power “is a major challenge.”

Perschbacher addressed the protesters directly, saying Washington has some of the strictest environmental laws in the country and that the state’s data center work group reinforced those rules rather than weakening them. Bills on ratepayer protections and transparency for data centers are likely to come back in the next legislative session, he said.

The issue also came up in the event’s second panel, on AI policy. State Sen. Marko Liias, who sponsored a bill this year on high-risk uses of AI, said data centers that want to locate in Washington need to meet “stringent expectations,” including adding clean energy to the grid, recycling water and dropping nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark. Washington’s goal “has never been to be the cheapest or easiest place,” he said.

“When energy becomes scarce, I do think we need to be clear that our communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do,” Liias said.

Joe Braidwood, founder of AI governance startup Glacis, which works out of AI House, said on the same panel that it was the first event he’d attended there with a public protest. “I think that’s actually kind of promising that people care enough to want to come together and talk and disagree and figure this out,” he said.

Zazueta, OpenAI’s global head of community programs, said in the opening panel that the industry needs to do a better job showing people the benefits of AI. Many people “read about these scary headlines,” she said, but don’t see how the technology applies to their daily lives.

OpenAI runs AI literacy workshops and trains libraries and community groups to lead their own, she said. The company opened an expanded office in Bellevue in March, its largest engineering center outside San Francisco.

Speaking with GeekWire outside the event on Monday afternoon, one of the protesters who had interrupted the panel singled out that remark. She said it dismissed public concerns about AI as the product of bad headlines, and she objected to the idea of using community groups to win people over to the benefits of artificial intelligence.

“They want to infiltrate our communities,” she said.

The opening panel with Zazueta, Perschbacher and Nguyen was titled “The Abundance State: Washington’s Chance to Lead the AI Future.” The protester objected to that framing, saying the panelists’ idea of abundance came down to easing permits for data centers.

It wasn’t the first time the group has protested the tech industry’s energy use. In 2024, it blocked entrances at Amazon’s Seattle headquarters to protest the company’s plans to power data centers in Oregon with natural gas.

Inside the event on Monday, as the interruptions continued, Nguyen, a former state senator who now leads the Seattle chamber, had responded to the protesters directly. “If you want to have your own event, have your own event,” he told them.

After they were led out, Nguyen said he agreed with the protesters, calling their passion “very warranted.” Those concerns are one reason Washington created some of the most stringent energy policies in the country, he said, adding that everyone would be better off if data centers elsewhere were held to the same standards.

“I think we’re very unique in Washington state to be able to actually do this in a way that really is mindful of our values, of the environment, and also pushing for innovation as well,” he said.

At the same time, Nguyen said demand for AI and data centers is market-driven, and it isn’t fair to criticize data centers while using them every day.

“For anybody who’s upset with data centers, I hope that when you email me, don’t email me,” he said. “Print it off and walk it to my office.”

Update, Oct. 27: Protesters interrupted the opening session of WTIA’s Seattle AI Summit six times Tuesday morning, during an on-stage interview of OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji by GeekWire’s Todd Bishop. They objected to AI-related job losses, the climate impact of data centers, OpenAI’s ties to the Trump administration and the leadership of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

#5549. Google finds ‘LLMjacking’ attackers running up $100K a day in fraudulent cloud charges

A new report out today from Google LLC’s Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that attackers who hijack enterprise access to large language models are running up fraudulent cloud charges of more than $100,000 in a single day.

The report, “The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources,” covers multiple LLMjacking cases Mandiant responded to this year. At some organizations, the cumulative bill reached $1 million before access was revoked.

Cryptojacking, the older way of stealing cloud compute, tends to drain resources gradually. LLMjacking charges can spike in a matter of hours.

Victims in North America, South America and Asia-Pacific included financial services and retail companies, along with technology and transportation businesses. GTIG has tied the intrusions to several financially motivated clusters and sees a growing split between the people who break in and the operators who resell the access.

In most of the investigations, attackers got in with cloud identity credentials that had been stolen or left exposed, including service account keys and GitHub personal access tokens. Others went after LLM endpoints left open to the internet, such as exposed Ollama servers.

A group tracked as UNC6993 broke into a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used that foothold to reach an LLM application programming interface. A fake portal it hosted posed as a sign-up page for a group of LLM users. Visitors were sent to the real LLM service and told to paste back a raw JSON payload containing an active access token. With that token, passwords and multifactor authentication no longer stood in the way.

Another actor scraped LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and tested each one with a request capped at a single output token. Requests that small slipped under the volume-based alerts in the victims’ security monitoring tools.

Routing software is a target too. In one case a follow-on cluster obtained pre-validated virtual keys from the group that had established access, then exploited a user ID rebind flaw in LiteLLM’s key regeneration endpoint. The bug, CVE-2026-40217, let it turn ordinary virtual keys into master administrator credentials for the victim’s gateway.

Some of the stolen access was burned through directly. UNC6993 tried to generate more API keys and switch on extra services inside victim cloud projects, and the charges quickly passed $100,000. A different actor signed victim accounts up for pay-as-you-go agreements on premium models. To get around rate limits, the actor used what GTIG calls a “burn and rotate” strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts.

A third went further and planted a containerized backdoor built on the Manus agent framework, which asked an upstream model to reason through instructions and then executed the resulting commands on the compromised host.

Other access ends up for sale through what GTIG calls “LLM Mixers.” These operations run stolen credentials through open-source API gateways and custom relays so usage can be metered and the origin of each request hidden. UNC6993 used tools such as new-api and gcli2api, likely to pool stolen keys, and GTIG believes the group sells access through underground storefronts.

One mixer is Jet Night, a token routing service. An actor that made more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours was using stolen third-party keys to power it, and one victim organization was left with nearly $1 million in token costs.

Jet Night sells an unlimited plan claiming frontier model access for about $60 a month. Comparable consumer plans typically cost $100 to $250, and GTIG thinks prices that low only work on stolen keys. Outages advertised on the service’s Telegram channel are likely the result of victims finding the compromise and revoking keys.

GTIG expects attackers increasingly to favor LLMjacking over cryptojacking because the mixers pay out quickly and at high margins. Exposed API tokens and model routing middleware will draw more automated targeting as companies put higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production, the report predicts.

On the defensive side, the report notes that in several of Mandiant’s cases, the victim had never enabled LLM services. Attackers used stolen keys to turn on services such as Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Amazon Bedrock and Google’s Gemini API, and a bill could balloon within minutes from there.

Any unauthorized enablement should be treated as a critical security event, it says. Spending caps, API keys scoped to specific models and environments and log monitoring for the single-token pings used to validate stolen keys are among its other recommendations.

Threat actors want artificial intelligence to give them scale over defenders, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, and they are getting it with agentic tools and tokens stolen from unwitting third parties.

“Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks,” Hultquist said.

#5547. Open Real Estate gets a boost from independents — and an opening from MLSs

Open Real Estate said it has secured 826 letters of support from brokerage leaders nationwide, including 493 from independent firms. Several MLS executives publicly welcomed dialogue, positioning the effort as complementary to existing MLS infrastructure.  AI Summary

A week after Open Real Estate, a broker-led initiative to build a shared infrastructure for residential listing data, launched, the initiative announced that it has secured 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders across the country.

Independent firms account for the majority of that backing, with 493 letters, or 59%, coming from independent brokerages, according to an announcement on Monday. Support spans single-office independents to some of the largest independent firms, including Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

The effort is designed as a national, shared data layer that connects brokerages, agents, multiple listing services and real estate portals. Founding organizations include AGNT Inc. (parent to eXp Realty and NextHome), HomeServices of America, Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

“We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founding members of Open Real Estate said in a joint statement.

Open Real Estate’s backers say the project is meant to complement, not replace, existing MLS organizations by expanding access to listing information for brokerages, agents and consumers.

Several prominent MLS executives publicly welcomed collaboration with the initiative.

“We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Brian Donnellan, the president and CEO of Bright MLS and a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement.

Art Carter, CEO of California Regional MLS (CRMLS), added that the effort aligns with CRMLS’s long-running work to give brokers more flexibility in how they input and manage listing data.

“Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform. It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability,” Carter, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.”

North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS) CEO Chris Carrillo framed Open Real Estate as part of a broader conversation about transparency and equal access to listings.

“NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” Carrillo said.

And NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain emphasized that broker-driven projects can coexist with MLSs.

“Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” Dain, also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.”

The push for a shared listing data infrastructure comes as the industry adapts to rapid changes in how listings are distributed and displayed, ongoing antitrust scrutiny and shifting brokerage business models. Brokerages are looking for more direct control over how their listing data flows to MLSs, portals, internal systems and third-party tools.

Open Real Estate’s founders position the initiative as a way to streamline listing distribution, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace, particularly as consumer expectations for transparent, real-time listing information continue to rise.

#5546. Who’s getting Anthropic’s compute spending? IPO filing shows where the tech giants really stand

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 6:53 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:58 am

Anthropic’s IPO filing reads like a ledger of who’s getting paid in the AI boom. The Seattle region’s tech giants are on the list, but they aren’t at the top.

The prospectus, filed Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission, details more than $750 billion in computing deals, including firm commitments and estimated future spending, and offers clues about what its founders and biggest investors stand to gain ahead of the company’s planned Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT.

Amazon and Microsoft have invested billions in Anthropic and won high-profile spending commitments from the Claude maker. But both trail Google, chipmaker Broadcom and Elon Musk’s SpaceX in their shares of Anthropic’s planned spending on computing power, the filing shows.

Following the compute money: Google’s chips are the biggest winner. Anthropic has lined up roughly $400 billion in computing capacity, mostly over the next seven years, based on Google-designed AI chips, known as tensor processing units or TPUs.

That total includes $114.5 billion to Google directly through July 2033, $161.2 billion in equipment leases with chipmaker Broadcom, and an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion in additional TPU capacity from 2028 to 2031.

Broadcom’s leases are the largest single arrangement in the filing. The five-year leases provide TPU-based hardware for data centers operated by other companies on Anthropic’s behalf.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is next. Anthropic agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion through 2029 for computing capacity from SpaceX’s AI subsidiary, formerly known as xAI, which runs a rival AI lab.

The filing says payments will reach about $3.1 billion a month once all the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December. The agreements run into 2029, though either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice after early 2027.

Amazon is still a big winner. Anthropic committed in April to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon Web Services over 10 years, through April 2036, and AWS Trainium is one of four chip families that Anthropic uses to train and run its models.

Microsoft’s piece is smaller, which reflects its later start. The company was aligned closely with OpenAI for years before striking its own deal with Anthropic.

Anthropic has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud from November 2026 through May 2033, the filing shows. That’s up from the $30 billion Azure deal announced in November 2025. The deal has been amended twice since, most recently this month.

Claude is built into Microsoft 365, and former Microsoft CFO Chris Liddell joined Anthropic’s board in February.

Two smaller providers have deals in the same range as Microsoft’s. Anthropic agreed to spend up to about $44.6 billion with Nscale, a U.K.-based AI infrastructure company, and about $41.3 billion with GPU cloud provider Lambda, both for capacity powered by Nvidia chips, according to the filing.

Will Anthropic need it all? Most of the commitments can’t be canceled, and the deals with Microsoft, Google and Amazon require Anthropic to pay “regardless of actual usage,” according to the filing.

So far, the demand is there. Anthropic’s revenue hit $11.6 billion in the second quarter, up from $787 million a year earlier, and the company posted its first operating profit, $974 million. It still had a $66.3 billion net loss, mostly from accounting charges tied to its soaring valuation.

The company says it has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.”

Its compute commitments assume that demand keeps growing. Anthropic spent less than $2 billion a month on compute and infrastructure in the second quarter. The SpaceX deal alone is expected to cost about $3.1 billion a month at full capacity.

Paper fortunes: Amazon’s biggest payoff is its stake, which it valued at $190.4 billion as of June 30 in its quarterly SEC filing. That includes convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal that Amazon valued at $97.9 billion. The notes would convert into stock, subject to a 12% ownership cap that Amazon can waive.

Amazon is scheduled to report third-quarter results Thursday, its first earnings report since Anthropic’s filing. The Seattle-based company has updated the value of its Anthropic holdings in each of its quarterly filings this year, so a new number could come this week.

Google put $10 billion into Anthropic’s latest funding round and can invest up to $20 billion more under a March financing deal. The filing doesn’t give ownership percentages for Amazon, Google or Microsoft. It says only that the three companies have each made “significant equity investments” in Anthropic.

Anthropic’s seven co-founders hold roughly 230 million to 245 million shares each, worth about $14 billion apiece at the latest private funding price. The company also gave its own Public Benefit Fund about 847 million shares, or 5% of its fully diluted stock as of June 30, worth about $50 billion at that price.

Anthropic could begin formally marketing its IPO to investors as soon as the week of Nov. 9, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is aiming to go public the following week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The company expects the offering to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, according to Bloomberg. SpaceX raised $75 billion in June, the largest IPO on record.

#5545. On theCUBE Pod: Stock market gets the jitters and Anthropic files IPO

The hubbub at the New York Stock Exchange was audible on theCUBE Pod last Friday, with concerns rising over the artificial intelligence bubble.

Several tech companies, including Intel Corp., Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com Inc., CoreWeave Inc. and Fortinet Inc., saw their stock fall, suggesting that investors may have doubts about all that AI infrastructure spending. At the same time, Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which looks to be a grand debut for one of the biggest AI developers out there (despite the company still not turning a profit).

Also causing a stir is the announcement that NYSE parent company, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), will partner with Trade[XYZ] to bring perpetual futures markets built on cryptocurrency trading platform, Hyperliquid, to the U.S., subject to regulatory approval.

“The whole idea of exchange is going to change,” said John Furrier (pictured, left), executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “It reminds me of cloud computing, how it re-leveled the data center. NYSE is the cathedral of capitalism. Nasdaq started as an over-the-counter bulletin board. Tech was early there and then only listed there. But now the game has changed. It’s very interesting to see how the competition between the NYSE and the Nasdaq is going to play out.”

On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (right), chief analyst at theCUBE Research, discussed what Anthropic’s IPO and Friday’s stock market jitters suggest about a potential AI bubble. They also explored Intel’s missteps and the opportunity for full-stack infrastructure companies.

Last week, Alphabet’s stock fell more than 12% after it reported slower growth in search revenue, presumably because chatbots are drawing people away from the browser. Amazon also had a disappointing Friday, with its stock falling 7% as the company continues to dump money into an AI infrastructure buildout.

Despite investors’ concerns, Vellante sees the AI bubble letting out a little air. He views this as a healthy sign for the AI market’s future.

“Think of the tulip bubbles in the 1600s,” Vellante said. “Think about the Japanese real estate bubble in the 1980s. And you think about the dot-com. That dot-com was actually different. Dot-com, they were all … overhyped. They drove massive valuations. But the dot-com actually played out. It actually exceeded expectations. And I think there’s some things that we can learn from there.”

Furrier sees evidence for a positive growth cycle, starting with cloud growth, which is needed to support the AI expansion. He also suggested that the infrastructure boom could coexist with the neocloud shakeout, as enterprise AI starts to create jobs rather than taking them away. Last week isn’t necessarily indicative of the AI bubble popping any time soon, he argues.

“Rationale is kicking in, common sense,” he said. “You’re starting to see the beginning of a transition. Wall Street is trying to figure it out. I think they don’t yet get it. But if you look at the language of the experts on the inside and how all the IPOs are being positioned, the value of these IPOs — they want durability. That transition from Silicon Valley tech ecosystem platforms is going to move into the markets. This is a platform game.”

Intel stock saw the steepest drop last week, almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report. The company has leaned into CPUs over GPUs, which Vellante thinks is missing the mark; the real game is not CPUs versus GPUs, but rather AI platforms. Nonetheless, he and Furrier predict Intel will make up some ground.

“Lip-Bu Tan and Intel have an opportunity,” Furrier said. “You basically lost the hyperscaler market that they once had a foothold in. You still run x86 on some clusters. But they got to look at other footprints. I think he’ll turn it around. It’s a multiyear journey, as he says. But the fact of the matter is why I don’t think it’s a bubble, is companies like Alphabet dropping major, major action, $500 billion, in a day.”

Intel is just one component in a rapidly changing ecosystem. Although the AI boom draws comparisons to the bubbles of yore, theCUBE concluded that this is still a unique phenomenon the market has to grapple with, and one that will play out over decades.

“This is just a natural adoption phase,” Vellante said. “What’s different is a lot of things. Like you said, tech is suddenly deflationary. We’re trading CapEx for labor, and that hasn’t really kicked in yet. We’re seeing individual productivity gains but it hasn’t shown up at the firm level yet. These things just take time. And, of course, Wall Street’s like, show me the money.”

#5543. Could dual licensing grow as agents, LOs seek revenue opportunities?

A RETR analysis identified 3,729 potential matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers, highlighting interest in dual licensing as professionals seek additional income. Shawn McNeil, a real estate broker and mortgage originator, said holding both licenses gives him greater control over clients' financing options and another source of revenue.  AI Summary

As mortgage companies and real estate brokerage look for additional revenue to combat difficult housing market conditions, dual licensing offers professionals a way to earn income through the tasks of selling a home and originating a mortgage.

A recently published analysis by RETR identified 3,729 matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers in which the agent’s top loan officer shared the agent’s name. California accounted for 40% of these matches, while the top four states (which also include Florida, Texas and Arizona) represented nearly 71% of dual-licensed professionals.

RETR used name matching to identify agents whose top-producing loan officer shared their name. But the analysis does not independently verify dual licensure, and it excludes professionals who hold both licenses but do not originate mortgages for their own clients or primarily work in one role.

For Shawn McNeil, the broker/owner of HomeFlo and a loan officer for Mpire Financial Group, the decision to pursue both licenses came from wanting more control over his clients’ financing options.

After nine years in real estate, McNeil obtained his MLO license about 18 months ago after what he described as feeling frustrated watching friends and high-value clients turn to large lenders and receive unfavorable interest rates.

“I would watch my big, high-dollar, personal friends go to these big-box retailers and just get absolutely crushed with an interest rate,” McNeil said in an interview with HousingWire. “I was like, at first, I’m going to go get licensed so that I can talk through these things and be knowledgeable in this.”

McNeil estimates that his time spent between real estate and loan originating is about 50/50, with most business coming from friends and real estate investors. He occasionally serves as both the agent and lender in a transaction, although he said that is not common.

McNeil believes more real estate agents will pursue MLO licenses as market conditions remain challenging and AI tools make it easier to research mortgage guidelines and loan requirements.

He said agents often hear that loan officers make good partners, but they may not fully understand the mortgage process or what makes a lender a good fit until they gain experience themselves.

“I think more agents are going to realize that the job on the loan officer side is getting easier from a guideline standpoint, and I think that they’re going to more and more convert to doing both over time,” McNeil said.

McNeil clarified that he does not originate every loan for clients who work with his brokerage. He refers borrowers to other lenders when his mortgage company cannot offer a particular program or when a loan falls outside his expertise.

Dual licensing also requires attention to compensation arrangements, the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA), state licensing rules and loan program restrictions.

McNeil said he worked with legal counsel to establish disclosures, which inform all brokerage clients that he is a licensed loan officer and owns the real estate brokerage, regardless of whether they use his mortgage services.

“We require 100% disclosure. … Even if you’re not using my services, we still disclose to you that I am a licensed loan officer and I own the real estate brokerage,” he said, adding that his clients receive the disclosures electronically before a transaction goes under contract.

RETR’s analysis does not establish whether dual licensing is becoming more common or how profitable the model is. But McNeil expects more agents to consider it as they look for additional income opportunities.

“I just hope that the trend continues and more and more realize that there’s a huge opportunity to do both,” he said.

#5542. Nuclear power at sea: Seattle startup targets Norway for ships and floating power plants

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:06 amOctober 27, 2026 at 7:15 am

Emerald Nuclear today announced a $2.1 million award from The Research Council of Norway to support its efforts to bring nuclear energy to the shipping industry and offshore power. The Seattle-based startup is developing high-temperature gas reactors that use an encapsulated fuel designed to resist meltdowns.

“This award will enable Emerald Nuclear to work directly with our marine partners to validate integration of our technology with their state-of-the-art marine power distribution and control systems,” said Wesley Deason, co-founder and CEO.

The funding supports Norway’s Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project, which is being led by Emerald Nuclear’s Norwegian subsidiary.

Shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, making it a significant target for lower-carbon energy solutions. Some ferries serving shorter routes are adopting hybrid-electric propulsion. Shipping companies are exploring methanol, ammonia, biofuels and other alternatives to heavy fuel oil, but their climate benefits depend on how those fuels are produced and used.

Nuclear reactors have powered U.S. Navy submarines for more than 70 years. Now, a new wave of companies is working to expand nuclear power’s role in commercial shipping and other marine applications.

The award supports an early development step for Emerald Nuclear, with substantial work remaining before commercial deployment. The company has yet to build its first reactor, and its plans will require additional financing, regulatory approvals and a reliable fuel supply. The startup has previously received an undisclosed amount of funding from angel investors.

Emerald Nuclear has five employees, most of them in Norway, and is targeting two applications: offshore ships that help construct facilities like oil platforms and wind turbines and lay deep-sea cables, and floating power plants for remote communities. Each reactor is designed to produce 5 megawatts (6,705 horsepower), according to the company.

Bringing nuclear to the marine environment poses several significant challenges. They include safety issues, regulations for vessels traveling internationally, management of nuclear fuel and waste, and the way shipping companies frequently buy and sell vessels.

Deason said the company’s approach helps address those concerns:

Emerald Nuclear is designing its technology “to integrate with the unique power needs of the ship, but also to meet the ways that the maritime industry does business,” Deason said.

Other companies pursuing nuclear ship propulsion include Core Power, newcleo and Blykalla. Core Power, Westinghouse, Saltfoss Energy and Prodigy Clean Energy are also developing floating nuclear power stations. Russia’s state-owned Rosatom already has nuclear-powered icebreakers and a floating nuclear power plant in operation.

Prior to launching Emerald Nuclear, Deason, a nuclear engineer, worked for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp. (USNC) developing reactors for space-based applications.

During his tenure at the Seattle company, a professor from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology approached USNC about applications for the maritime sector. USNC declared bankruptcy in October 2024 and the deal wasn’t pursued. But the idea interested Deason and Hallgeir Juliebø, a Norwegian entrepreneur who had been a consultant with USNC. The two co-founded Emerald Nuclear in 2024 and Juliebø serves as chief commercial officer.

Emerald Nuclear has signed a lease for an engineering center in Norway, where it’s designing and building its first prototype, a non-nuclear thermal device that will be used for the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project.

Other partners for the project are VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk, bringing together nuclear technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations and academic research.

The startup will build its first nuclear reactor, named the Gem Microreactor, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, with 2030 as its goal for completion. Emerald Nuclear will integrate equipment from Peregrine Turbine Technologies in Maine to convert the reactor’s heat into electricity.

The target for the first commercial deployment is 2031, on a Norwegian offshore vessel.

Deason is hoping to open a manufacturing site in the future in Western Washington on Puget Sound with an initial focus on floating nuclear power systems that replace diesel generators. That phase of growth is roughly targeted to the early 2030s.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5541. Marvell to acquire optical component maker Lumentum in massive $115B deal

Marvell Technology Inc. today announced plans to acquire Lumentum Holdings Inc. for $115 billion, in one of the largest deals in tech history.

Lumentum investors are set to receive 4.5 Marvell shares for every unit of stock they own. That translates to about $1,132 per share, which is 23.9% higher than the company’s last unaffected stock price.

Investors, however, weren’t so sanguine about the deal. Marvell’s shares fell almost 13%, while Lumentum’s fell almost 19%. Chalk it up, again, to recent investor worry that the promised growth from artificial intelligence infrastructure may not last forever.

Marvell provides networking equipment for data centers and telecommunications infrastructure. Many of its products use fiber-optic cables to transmit data. Lumentum, in turn, makes components for fiber-optic network devices such as those offered by Marvell. The acquisition will give the latter company more control over its supply chain, which could enable it to more closely align upstream components’ design with its requirements.

Optical networks use laser emitters to generate the light which they transmit data. Lumentum sells a line of lasers based on indium phosphide, a semiconducting material that generates light more efficiently than silicon. The product family includes modular and continuous wave devices. Modulated lasers are used to physically connect servers to the host data center’s optical network, while continuous wave lasers power longer-range network links.

Lumentum also makes single-mode optical amplifiers. Such devices strengthen the laser signals that travel through long-haul carrier networks to reduce data transmission errors.

Last year, the company debuted a laser optimized for co-packaged optics, or CPO, chips. Such chips enable servers to connect to the host data center’s network without expensive modules called transceivers that are usually needed for the task. CPO technology has emerged as an important focus of Marvell’s growth strategy. Its chip design business can help customers integrate CPO modules into their custom artificial intelligence accelerators.

Lumentum doesn’t focus solely on the laser component market. It uses a material called indium gallium arsenide to make analog photodetectors, which customers can use to monitor their optical networks for errors. The company also sells optical circuit switches. Such devices use tiny mirrors to coordinate the flow of traffic, which removes the need to turn data into electrical signals and thereby saves power.

Notably, Lumentum will also give Marvell a presence in the industrial equipment market. The former company makes high-power lasers for cutting and welding machines. It’s unclear what will happen to that part of Lumentum’s product portfolio following the deal. After a large acquisition, companies sometimes spin off newly absorbed business units that don’t align with their core focus.

“By bringing together two leaders with highly complementary technologies, exceptional talent and specialized manufacturing capabilities, we intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value,” said Marvell Chief Executive Officer Matt Murphy.

The chipmaker expects to close the acquisition in the first half of 2028. The combined company will be led by Murphy, while Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston will join the board along with two of the optical component supplier’s directors.

Marvell expects the deal to become accretive to its adjusted earnings per share within a year of closing. In the longer term, the company hopes to achieve annual run-rate cost savings of more than $1 billion and accelerate revenue growth. Marvell estimates that Lumentum will expand its total addressable market to $550 billion.

#5539. Real estate is moving toward more data privacy. Appraisers say UAD 3.6 is moving the other way

UAD 3.6 takes effect Monday, requiring appraisers to use dropdown selections that standardize property details sent to the GSEs. Appraisers are focused on Certification 25, which expands downstream rights to store, analyze, and distribute report data, including interior photos.  AI Summary

Monday marks the implementation date of UAD 3.6, which requires appraisers to select specific data points from dropdown menus for every feature of a property, as opposed to writing text descriptions of the home as they previously did, increasing the amount of detail included in appraisal reports delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Within UAD 3.6 is the new Certification 25, which has generated quite the buzz among appraisal professionals.

Certification 25, which was established by the government sponsored entities (GSEs), expands the data reuse beyond the parameters set in UAD 2.6, which included Certification 21, which largely governed who could receive or distribute a physical appraisal report.

Under Certification 25, entities that receive appraisal reports like lenders, GSEs, secondary market participants and data collection services to store, copy, reproduce, analyze, use and distribute all data within the report, including interior photos and property details, for internal or external purposes without needing the appraiser’s further consent.

While the certification does state that the appraiser and supervisory appraiser bear no liability for any use of the report outside of the specific mortgage finance transaction, appraisers are still concerned about this change and how it could impact their relationship with brokerages and real estate professionals.

In posts on social media and articles written on Appraisers Blog, Desiree Mehbod, a Virginia-based appraiser, has raised concerns about what would happen if interior photos of a child’s bedroom with the property address are leaked, reproduced and shared, ultimately ending up on the dark web.

But the ability for downstream actors to have access to data like this is not new. According to Frank Gregoire, a Florida-based appraiser, Certification 25 is fairly similar to the statute it is replacing, Certification 21.

“Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac maintain a proprietary database about every single dwelling that has ever had a loan on it,” Gregoire said. “So, the ability for downstream users to have access to that data has been there since these forms were introduced in the early 2000s. But, what is new is that it now specifies that the appraiser is aware that some parties may be using the data from their reports without their permission.”

While Ryan Lundquist agrees that this is the only primary change with Certification 25, he still finds it incredibly concerning.

“They can take the information and share it with whoever they want and the appraiser doesn’t have any control over that,” Lundquist, a Sacramento-based appraiser, said. “I know a lot of appraisers feel conflicted about that as it feels like it puts appraisers in a tough spot where a blank check to mine whatever data they want exists.”

Lundquist said he would love to know who this information will be shared with or sold to.

Gregoire is also concerned about appraisers including copyrighted data, such as images in the MLS in their report.

“If the appraiser is an MLS participant, they are using that information under license and they are permitted to use it to support their valuation, but that is it, they cannot grant someone else the right to use that information and that is what’s happening with Certification 25,” he said.

It is concerns like these that lead appraisers to say the discussion around Certification 25 is not over yet.

“I don’t think it will sit well with a lot of people in real estate when they read or begin to understand how and where this data may be used,” Lundquist said.

In addition, Mehbod said Certification 25  is why she and other like-minded appraisers have chosen to stop doing appraisal work for the GSEs. If a homebuyer wants their loan to close they have no choice but to allow the appraiser to generate a report, which Mehbod said will create “massive animosity right at the front door.”

“It positions the appraiser as a forced data collector rather than an independent expert,” she said. “This friction damages public trust and opens a legal minefield for our profession, leaving appraisers highly vulnerable to consumer complaints and lawsuits from angry borrowers when transactions get messy over data harvesting policies they never wanted to participate in.”

With UAD 3.6 just beginning to go into effect, it remains to be seen if anything regarding Certification 25 will change or how consumers and real estate brokers, agents and MLSs will respond.

#5538. Seattle startup Avante raises $30M to bring AI agents to corporate benefits teams

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 27, 2026 at 9:03 amOctober 27, 2026 at 9:29 am

Avante, the maker of an AI platform to help companies manage employee health care and other benefits, has landed a $30 million Series A round.

Frist Cressey Ventures led the round, with participation from Sorenson Capital, Hearst Ventures, Morgan Stanley Next Level Fund and existing investor Fuse. The new funding, announced Tuesday, brings Seattle-based Avante’s total raised to $40 million, following a $10 million seed round led by Fuse in 2024.

Benefits are one of employers’ biggest costs. Avante’s AI agents do work like comparing vendor contracts against actual claims, reviewing plan documents for errors and preparing for renewals. Employees can also use the platform to ask questions about their own coverage.

The startup plans to use the cash to expand internationally and develop more AI agents, building on a beta release of its “Ava Agents” last week.

Avante says it now has more than 70 customers, including Samsung Semiconductor, Real Chemistry, Zscaler and News Corp, and that bookings grew nearly fivefold over the past year. The platform reaches more than 385,000 employees and family members, according to the company.

Avante was founded in 2023 by CEO Rohan D’Souza; Carly Eckert, a physician and epidemiologist who serves as head of innovation and impact; and executive chairman Kabir Shahani, the co-CEO of Amperity.

D’Souza and Eckert previously worked as executives at health care automation company Olive AI, which shut down in 2023. The startup emerged from stealth in early 2024 and launched publicly in April 2025.

“Benefits teams are responsible for one of the largest and most consequential investments their companies make, yet they’re still operating with outdated information, archaic spreadsheets, and technology built for another era,” D’Souza said in a statement.

Avante is pitching its software as employers face rising health care costs. Large employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase for 2027, the company said.

The startup competes with benefits and HR software providers such as Workday, ADP, Deel and Rippling. It has also signed partnerships with benefits advisory firms including Gallagher, OneDigital, Segal Benz, Howden and USI Insurance Services.

Avante ranks No. 156 on the GeekWire 200, our list of top Pacific Northwest tech startups.

#5537. Palantir beats Q3 forecasts as US commercial revenue overtakes government for first time

Shares of Palantir Technologies Inc. rose more than 1% in late trading today after the big-data analytics company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year revenue guidance for the third time this year.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Palantir reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, up from 21 cents in the same quarter of last year, on revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 41 cents per share on revenue of $2.18 billion. It was the first quarter in which Palantir’s revenue topped $2 billion.

U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time in Palantir’s history. Sales to commercial customers in the U.S. reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Government sales rose 96%, to $953 million. Together they took total U.S. revenue to $1.937 billion, up 119% year-over-year.

Palantir closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million in the quarter, including 64 worth $10 million or more. Total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, to $2.918 billion, after growing 151% in the same period of 2025. U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79%, to $6.517 billion.

Net income more than doubled, to $1.128 billion from $476 million a year earlier, giving the company a 49% net margin. On an adjusted basis, operating income came to $1.427 billion at a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. Palantir’s “Rule of 40” score hit 158%. The company ended September holding $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and U.S. Treasury securities.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Karp used the earnings release to argue that what he called the “Sovereign AI movement” is creating “the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots” he has seen in 30 years in business. Governments and companies alike are being forced into one group or the other, “voluntarily or not,” according to Karp. That shift, he said, is “purpose-built for Palantir.”

Looking to the fourth quarter, Palantir expects revenue of $2.649 billion to $2.653 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.640 billion to $1.644 billion. Analysts had forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $2.46 billion.

Full-year revenue guidance now stands at $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion, up from the $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion Palantir forecast in August. U.S. commercial revenue is expected to exceed $3.559 billion, growth of at least 143%, and the company lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to a range of $5.245 billion to $5.249 billion. Adjusted free cash flow for 2026 is now forecast at $4.8 billion to $5 billion.

#5535. Anthropic Claude AI Predicts an Unbelievable XRP Q4 Move

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts a frankly insane XRP price target by January 1, 2027. Somewhere in its notes, there’s a number. It’s a market cap in the trillions, contingent on a hypothetical catalyst for Ripple that could see it flip Ethereum as the market’s second-largest digital asset.

XRP price is sitting around $1.29, after drifting down from a roughly $1.50 open. Spot ETF inflows have dried up, sentiment is sleepy, and the next support level is $1.25. That’s what makes it the perfect time for an out-there prediction.

It’s the first week of December. After a closed-door summit, a coalition of G20 central banks announces in a joint communiqué that its cross-border CBDC settlement network will use the XRP Ledger as its neutral bridge layer.

XRP is named the default bridge asset for settling between currencies without a direct corridor. Think of it as the “SWIFT moment” XRP maximalists have dreamed about for a decade, except it happens in public, with official signatures, and with no hedge language.

How likely is it? Very unlikely. Central banks move at the speed of committees, and sovereigns dislike depending on assets they don’t control. But it’s not physically impossible, which is the whole game here.

Then the dominoes fall. Treasury desks scramble for liquidity, sovereign wealth funds ask their prime brokers an awkward question about “operational inventory,” and a market with roughly 62 billion tokens in circulation meets demand it has never seen.

On the weekly chart, XRP has spent months coiling between $1.25 support and a $1.57–$1.70 supply zone, which is a textbook compression pattern. Right now, the 50-day EMA sits below the 200-day, so the chart looks bearish.

In this scenario, that death cross turns into the most-hated bull trap in history. A weekly close above $1.70 would trigger stop-loss cascades from shorts, and reclaiming the $3.65 all-time high would leave the chart with no overhead resistance and no historical sellers to absorb the move.

Measuring the height of the multi-year base and projecting it upward gives a first target near $9. Fibonacci extensions from the 2025 cycle high, stretched into price discovery, put the 1.618 and 2.618 levels in double digits.

Momentum indicators would sit pinned in “overbought” for weeks, which is exactly how parabolic markets behave. Meanwhile, volume would explode, and the usual rule that overbought means sell would stop working.

#5534. Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:19 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:52 am

Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas, Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.

The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.

Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch. Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.

While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.

Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

#5533. A $20M fine stalks Los Angeles over delay of a new housing project

A letter warns Los Angeles it has 60 days to act on a 398-home plan in Woodland Hills. The attorney cites Housing Accountability Act exposure of at least $19.9 million in fines, plus attorney fees, costs, and potential compensatory damages.  AI Summary

Blocking a Los Angeles housing development over a mountain lion could cost the city $20 million or more and still fail to stop the project.

L.A. has 60 days to approve 398 homes at Woodland Hills Country Club or face a lawsuit that could cost it that much, according to a letter from the club’s attorney, Dave Rand, sent to the city Friday. A judge could order the city to pay punitive damages for the delay and rule that the development still must proceed, Rand confirmed with HousingWire TBD.

If the club prevails in its case for damages provided under the Housing Accountability Act, the city would owe fines of at least $19.9 million. It would also owe attorney’s fees, costs and compensatory damages.

The letter says that exposure “could therefore cost the city well in excess of $20 million.” Rand wrote that he can’t imagine the risk to taxpayers “is worth it.”

Rand wrote that the city’s denial violated both Assembly Bill 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act. The letter invokes AB 712, which extends any limitation period by 60 days from the letter’s date. That keeps the club’s legal options open while the city weighs its response.

Rand explained the fine math on social media. The base fine is $10,000 per unit for a violation, and $50,000 per unit for a finding of bad faith.

AB 712 raises the fine to an automatic $50,000 per unit if the city has lost in court at least once in the same housing element cycle. At $50,000 a unit, 398 homes come to the $19.9 million cited in the letter.

The letter includes a claim for damages, which follows an Oct. 23 ruling from the Second Appellate District. It held that a homeowner could seek damages when a city misses a mandatory permit deadline.

That case involved an accessory dwelling unit, not AB 2011. Legal scholars have said its reasoning could reach other ministerial housing laws, including the one Rand cites.

The state housing department has set a Nov. 25 deadline for Los Angeles to respond to its own letter. The department said it could refer the matter to the state attorney general.

Other California cities have backed down when the cost of continuing to dig their heels in became clear. Glendale’s council voted 4-1 last October to reject Trammell Crow Residential’s 682-unit plan for a former Sears store. The project included 72 very low-income units.

The state housing department issued a notice of violation Dec. 30. It warned of fines up to $34 million if the city did not reverse course. Glendale’s council reversed its denial in late January, three months after rejecting the project. No lawsuit was filed, but the developer’s attorney had called the case a “slam dunk” under the Housing Accountability Act.

Morgan Hill in Silicon Valley took a similar path. City officials settled with High Street Residential, a builder’s remedy developer, to avoid costly litigation with the developer and the state.

The 105-home project had been hanging in legal limbo for three years. The city council unanimously approved it last week.
