#5515. AI Can Build Your Product in a Day —Here’s How Founders Get Someone to Actually Pay for It

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lessons from 500 first-time founders on how they landed their first paying customer, and how they built momentum.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This summer, more than 500 people from more than 50 countries joined an eight-week startup camp my company runs. Most had never started a business. Many had never written a line of code, and it didn’t matter. With today’s AI tools, most of them had a working product within the first couple of weeks.

Getting someone to pay was the hard part, and about 1 in 10 managed it.

I spent the weeks after camp asking those founders how they did it. This is what I learned:

Almost none of the first customers were strangers. One founder, a marketing consultant, built a small ad tool for his own use. He showed it to a group of entrepreneurs he met with regularly because he thought it might help them. Those 10 became the first paying customers. Another founder built a language-learning app. Her first customer was a math teacher in Italy, the friend of a friend of a friend. Three introductions away sounds far, but each one carried a little trust, and that was enough.

If you are starting out, write down the 50 people who would take your call. Your first customer is more likely on that list than in an ad audience.

The founders who got paid often sold something that wasn’t really a product yet. A founder working on grief support ran her whole service through Instagram direct messages. She had more than 500 conversations before she built a website, and each conversation was both the product and the demo.

The language app founder did something similar. She got her first user on a video call, set her up personally, and promised to build what she needed. The customer bought an annual plan.

AI makes it tempting to build first because building is so easy now. But a working app doesn’t prove anyone wants it. A person paying for the rough version does. Find the smallest version of your core promise and start figuring out whether someone will pay for that.

I didn’t find a single founder whose first sale came from a stranger on a checkout page alone. The yes came from a text message, a phone call, a video call or showing up in person. One founder who used to run a car collision repair shop found that ads, websites and email never closed a sale for him. Knocking on doors and picking up the phone did. Funnels matter later. For the first customer, you are the funnel.

Many founders put their first few hundred dollars into social media ads. Most learned the same lesson: ads buy attention, not trust. One founder got more than 40 signups and zero buyers. The grief-support founder got clicks and traffic but no customers, because someone scrolling past an ad on a random Tuesday is not someone who needs help right now.

There was one clear exception. A founder with a golf swing app got his first customers through paid ads. My read is that golfers already know they have the problem and go looking for a fix. When your buyer already knows they have the problem, ads can work. When they don’t, you are paying to explain the problem and the product at the same time.

Sometimes the first sale is for something you didn’t mean to sell. The marketing consultant set out to build one business. The side tool he made for himself became the business. Slack was created the same way – as an internal tool in what used to be a gaming company. The former collision shop owner had a lesson from his old business that stuck with me. He closed about 90% of the people who came in, and he was never the cheapest. Many of them didn’t really want the repair. They wanted the insurance money from the claim, and he helped them get what they actually needed. Early conversations will tell you what people will pay for if you listen for what is implied, not just what is said.

AI has taken most of the cost out of building. What it hasn’t changed is that someone has to decide to trust you with their money. That’s why the first $100 matters far more than the amount. It’s the first proof that someone who owes you nothing values what you offer.

So before you build the next feature, ask a different question: Who already trusts me, and what could I sell them this week?

Building is nearly free. Being trusted is not.

#5514. Blue Origin leases former Bartell Drugs warehouse south of Seattle for new manufacturing site

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:25 amOctober 28, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

KING 5 first reported the news Tuesday, citing a state environmental application filed in September that lists Blue Origin Manufacturing LLC at the building’s address, 21202 24th Ave. S. A pre-application under review by the city indicates the property could be used for research and development of commercial satellites, the station reported.

Commercial real estate firm Newmark announced a lease for the entire building last week without naming the tenant.

“The manufacturing project that will be using this property is cutting-edge and we are excited about the job growth and possibilities that it represents for our region,” Newmark Executive Vice Chairman Thad Mallory said in a news release.

With roughly 33,000 residents, the small city of Des Moines is becoming something of an aerospace hub.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5513. A Country Club Built Around a Private Racetrack? Why Exclusive Experiences are the Biggest Trend Among The Wealthy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

APEX Motorclub is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, on a 280-acre facility with race tracks, skid pads and luxury trackside condos, and by offering lifetime memberships to families it taps into the wealthy’s growing interest in passing down passions, not just assets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As COO, Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”

The Club is a 280-acre facility featuring 2 race tracks, a six-acre skid pad, 96 trackside garage condos, a drivers’ lounge and a clubhouse.

The goal is to give motorsports enthusiasts a place to share that passion with others, including their family members. At the same time, the exclusive luxury landscape offers an escape from the pressure of running a billion-dollar company, as some of its members do.

“We’ve got members whose names are known,” Barba says. “They run global companies, plus some local entrepreneurs that built great businesses. Motorsports are interesting because they all share the joy, rather than expecting to be Mr. or Mrs. So and So when they’re out here. That’s part of the culture we’ve created.”

There are two primary membership types: Gold, a $70,000 initiation fee plus an annual $8,000 fee and Platinum, a $90,000 initiation fee plus an annual $15,000 fee. The two are similar, offering 240+ annual track days, transferable membership and family access, with Platinum offering event host days. They also recently introduced a one-year membership for $35,000 and an under-35 membership with a $25,000 initiation fee plus $4,500 annually.

“Motorsports is not a cheap endeavor,” Barba explains. “To run a car for a weekend out here, you go through tires, brakes and maintenance. Depending on the type of car, that cost can go up quite a bit.”

While APEX provides the location and platform, members must maintain their own cars. Some have small teams doing only the necessary maintenance, while others come to the track with five people analyzing the data behind each lap. Some look to shave milliseconds off their cornering, while others just want a place to let the fancy ride they just bought rip.

APEX’s business model includes partnerships with luxury car companies. They have a deal with Lexus, which brought out cars to join the APEX fleet. They also have a relationship with Aston Martin, which has an on-site presence in their garage condos. The local McLaren Scottsdale, one of the country’s highest-volume McLaren dealers, is a corporate member of the club.

Companies will also rent the tracks for events, including Ferrari, Mercedes and Porsche.

“It gives them a chance to put people who aren’t necessarily enthusiastic enough to join a club on a track to understand what the car can do,” Barba explains. According to him, 85% of the engineering in performance cars never shows up on the street. At APEX, someone might own their fourth Porsche 911 but never experience its full power until they get on the course with an instructor.

“The guy who buys or leases a Lamborghini to park at the valet is not a member of a motorsports club,” Barba says. “Our members tend to have more enthusiasm for the vehicles. Then there’s a whole different area of what level of racing they may want.”

While most members are interested in track time, Barba estimates about 20% take wheel-to-wheel racing seriously. For them, APEX runs an 11-race series with 10 to 25 people per race, depending on the car. “Some people love it and thrive on the competition and pushing the car. Others want to enjoy the tracking and their times, but not race,” Babra says.

What sets APEX apart from the competition is its family policy.

“If you join APEX, your spouse and kids are a part of it, and we don’t age them out,” Barba shares. “What we saw historically was that a lot of clubs would age kids out, and then they’d have to buy a membership. We want kids to stay as long as possible because it keeps parents, grandparents and everyone else engaged. So it’s a family membership because we want it to be a family experience.”

This plays into a larger theme among the wealthy: finding the “new inheritance.” Rather than passing down expensive paintings and big houses, rich parents want to give their kids something more meaningful and personal.

One option is their passions. “Members will talk about the first race car they had, the first time they reached a certain speed, or the first time they watched their child drive a car,” Barba says. “It’s a passion that passes down, and it connects back to what I believe is most potent about motorsports: the emotions.”

One example is the Bacon family. Seth Bacon had built a successful logistics business focused on organ donations and sold it. Looking for a way to spend more time with his teenage son Jace as he approached adulthood, he found an unexpected solution: racing.

“He was about to turn 16 and get his driver’s license. He’s getting a job. He was busy in school. He’s about to go off to college, and I thought this is that period where he’s beginning to separate himself from the nest,” Seth says. “I wanted an opportunity for us to still do something tight together.”

The two visited APEX to watch a few races. Before long, they bought a pair of Radical race cars and hit the track themselves.

“Instead of the son ignoring him at 16, they’re working together on racing,” Barba says with a laugh.

At Jace’s first race at another club in Nevada, father and son competed together, with Jace winning.

“It made a real impact on the dad that out there, his son is an equal with guys who are running billion-dollar companies,” Barba says.

The Bacons could take their cars to any track, but few offer the built-in community they’ve found at APEX.

“There’s a lot of senior drivers, a lot of retired professional drivers who are members there, and everywhere we go, they’re always checking in on him, asking about his career,” Seth says of Jace. “It really is more of a community of people who are willing to support one another, not only on track, but also, how did that business of yours go? Did you get that acquisition you were looking for? What do you need next?”

Business connections are great, but at the end of the day, APEX is about cars, community and competition. A hole-in-one is unforgettable, but the average day on the golf course doesn’t necessarily make the lifetime highlight reel. Driving a luxury race car at breakneck speeds on an open track? That’s an experience that’s not only incredible, but repeatable.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As COO, Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”

#5511. VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.

Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.

By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.

Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.

“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”

Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.

Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 9:51 amOctober 28, 2026 at 10:17 am

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Sievert will also leave the board’s Transaction Committee, according to a federal filing. His departure comes a year after he handed the CEO job to Srini Gopalan.

A company spokesperson said via email that the vice chair role was structured as a one-year term, adding that Sievert has “been a valued strategic advisor throughout the leadership transition, and we’re incredibly grateful for his contributions.”

T-Mobile said in the filing that his departure “is not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to its operations, policies or practices.”

Sievert joined T-Mobile in 2012 as executive vice president and chief marketing officer, the same year John Legere became CEO. He later became president and chief operating officer and was mentored by Legere before succeeding him as chief executive in 2020. He served as CEO for about five and a half years.

Sievert was a central figure in T-Mobile’s campaign to brand itself the “Un-carrier.” During his time at the company, T-Mobile grew from fewer than 30 million customers to more than 130 million by September 2025, a period that included its merger with Sprint.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

#5509. 4 Reasons Your Homepage Messaging Isn’t Converting (and How to Address Them)

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Why isn’t your homepage converting visitors into customers? Discover four common website messaging mistakes and how customer interviews can help fix them.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

Companies often explain their products from their own perspective. They highlight what they’ve built, everything their product can do and the benefits they assume customers care about. It often results in messaging like “The AI-native GTM platform powering Precision GTM at scale.”

But buyers have their own priorities, frustrations and concerns. If your homepage doesn’t address those, even a great product can struggle to convert.

Here are four common messaging mistakes and how to fix them.

Many companies want their homepage to communicate everything their product can do. They try to capture multiple use cases, features and benefits in a single headline, hoping to appeal to as many potential customers as possible.

The result is often vague messaging that promises to “streamline operations,” “boost productivity,” “help your business grow,” or vague slogans like “We’ll take care of your accounting so you can focus on your business.”

These statements may have some truth, but they’re unlikely to resonate with someone facing a specific, urgent problem. When you try to communicate everything, you risk saying nothing compelling enough to make a buyer act.

Consider a project management platform for marketing agencies. Its homepage might promise to “streamline projects and improve team productivity” or some version of that. But customer interviews could reveal that agency owners are particularly frustrated by missed deadlines that damage client relationships.

Now the company has a more specific message to lead with: “Deliver every client project on time, without constantly chasing your team for updates.”

That message is more likely to capture the attention of an agency owner who’s tired of apologizing to clients for late work. It connects with a problem they’re experiencing and have a reason to solve.

In my customer research work, I often find that what companies think customers value most differs from what actually motivates them to look for a solution.

To find your strongest message, interview recent customers or prospects. Ask what prompted them to start looking for a solution, what problem they were most eager to solve and why solving it became a priority.

Look for the single problem or desired outcome that most consistently motivates your ideal customers to act. Lead with that message on your homepage. You can use the rest of the page to communicate everything else your product offers.

Your biggest competitor isn’t always another company. Often, it’s the way your prospective customers already do things.

They might recognize the problem your product solves but have learned to live with it. Unless the cost of continuing becomes clear, they have little reason to make a change.

Imagine a software product that automates invoicing for agencies. Its homepage might say, “Automate invoicing and save time.” That’s a reasonable benefit, but it doesn’t fully communicate why the problem deserves attention.

Now consider the agency owner’s existing workflow. Project managers finish work, someone manually checks billable hours, invoices are created at the end of the month, and the finance team follows up on unpaid balances.

The consequences might include delayed invoices, missed billable work, slower payments and unnecessary administrative costs. These are much more compelling reasons to change.

Instead of simply promising automation, the homepage could explain how manual billing creates revenue leakage and cash flow problems.

To make the status quo feel costly, make its consequences visible.

Ask customers what happened before they adopted your solution. How much time did they spend on the problem? What mistakes occurred? What opportunities did they miss? What happened when they delayed fixing it?

Use their answers to communicate the business and emotional impact of the problem. Wherever possible, include real numbers, concrete examples and real-life anecdotes.

Even when visitors recognize the problem, they still need to understand how your solution will improve their situation.

Many homepages fall short here because they emphasize generic benefits or product capabilities without explaining how the product fits into the buyer’s actual workflow.

For example, an AI-powered customer support platform might highlight advanced language models, intelligent routing and automated workflows. But customer research might reveal that support managers primarily want to reduce the number of repetitive tickets their agents handle without compromising customer satisfaction.

They want to know which questions AI can resolve, when a human agent takes over and how the platform will connect with their existing help desk. The homepage should answer those deeper questions or help the reader easily find that guidance elsewhere on the website.

Rather than simply stating that the product “improves support efficiency,” it could walk visitors through a familiar scenario: A customer asks about an order, AI retrieves the relevant information, and the issue gets resolved without an agent getting involved.

A simple workflow illustration can make the value immediately understandable.

I’ve found that understanding a customer’s existing process is one of the most useful parts of customer interviews. It reveals not only which benefits matter but also which details buyers need to see before they can imagine using a product.

Ask customers to walk you through how they handled the problem before finding your solution and what changed afterward. Then build your messaging around those specific improvements.

Even when buyers see the value, they might hesitate because they’re uncertain about what happens next.

Will the product work for their business? Will implementation be difficult? Will their team actually use it? Can they trust your company to deliver? These concerns can prevent otherwise interested visitors from converting.

I frequently see websites use customer logos and testimonials as their main form of reassurance. Those elements help, but they don’t necessarily answer the specific questions making buyers hesitate.

A small business considering a new accounting platform, for example, might be far more concerned about migrating its financial data than whether the software has won an industry award.

Showing how migration works, explaining the support available and featuring a customer who successfully made the switch could do more to increase conversions.

The most effective reassurance addresses the risks your buyers actually perceive.

Interview customers about the concerns they had before purchasing. Ask what nearly stopped them, what reassured them and what information would have made their decision easier.

Use those insights to select the right customer stories, product demonstrations, guarantees, implementation details and FAQs for your homepage.

Improving homepage conversions doesn’t always require a complete redesign, more persuasive copywriting or another round of A/B testing. Sometimes, the most valuable starting point is a handful of conversations with recent buyers.

Ask what problem made them look for a solution, why they couldn’t continue with their existing approach, what convinced them your product was right and what almost prevented them from buying.

Their answers can help you build a homepage that speaks to a real priority, makes the cost of inaction clear, demonstrates relevant value and gives visitors the confidence to take the next step.

That’s a much stronger foundation for conversion than guessing which headline or call to action might perform better.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

#5508. Sweetgreen managers could earn more than $200,000 a year under a new pay plan, as the salad chain bets higher pay will lift sales

A fast-casual chain favored by the office lunch set is sweetening compensation packages for managers at its restaurants.

Starting next year, Sweetgreen managers will be eligible to earn more than $200,000 a year if they meet certain milestones set by the company. The new offering, which will be paid through a mix of base salary and equity, is intended to empower managers who contribute to the business’s success, and “[share] those wins with those that are driving it,” co-founder and CEO Jonathan Neman said.

Under the new incentive plan, Sweetgreen managers (known as “head coaches”) will see their base pay increase by up to 45% if they work at restaurants with higher sales volume. The company declined to specify how high sales need to be to meet this threshold.

When restaurants outperform their sales goals, managers will get a revenue share bonus from the upside, with the percentage increasing based on their tenure in the business. Managers can also continue to receive equity in the company based on their performance.

Base salary increases will go into effect in Q1 of 2027, while head coaches will start to receive bonuses based on store performance on a quarterly basis from Jan. 1, 2027, according to Sweetgreen.

How Sweetgreen is making the case for higher pay. Higher labor and related costs cut into Sweetgreen’s earnings for the quarter ending in June, accounting for 29% of revenue, up from 28% the year prior. Same-store sales and restaurant profits also declined that quarter compared to 2025. (Sweetgreen will report Q3 earnings on Nov. 5.)

Amid such economic pressures, Neman recognized that investing in additional compensation for managers “is definitely a bet.”“But the data supports that if we’re able to attract, retain, and incentivize better head coaches, that they will drive higher sales and better margins,” he added. Neman noted that while Sweetgreen is investing some money upfront to raise managers’ base salaries, most of the investment is contingent on their stores meeting certain performance targets.

“Typically the company would take more of that upside. Now we’re sharing in that upside with our team, but…we think that’s a good trade,” he said.

Zoom out. Sweetgreen isn’t the first fast-casual chain to bet big on its managers. Chipotle announced in 2021 that workers in its highest general manager position could earn $100,000, on average, as it sought to hang onto workers in a tight labor market. The burrito business doesn’t appear to have taken a financial hit from this move, as its restaurant operating margins have stayed between 23% and 26% in recent years. More than 85% of general managers at Chipotle were promoted internally in 2025, according to its 2026 proxy statement.

Neman said Sweetgreen took inspiration from chains like In-N-Out Burger, which recently confirmed that store managers can earn more than $200,000 on average, and Raising Cane’s, which grants monthly bonuses to managers based on sales, and said in 2024 it paid managers up to $175,000 annually.

In addition to business performance, Sweetgreen will be looking at metrics like team member turnover, “head coach stability” (i.e. whether managers stay in their stores), quality and experience scores, and internal mobility to determine whether this incentive program is working, Neman said.

#5507. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5506. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

#5505. The Systems Behind Your Business Are Changing Beneath the Surface — and Most Teams Haven’t Caught On

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The GTM stack is getting an operating system. Most teams don’t know they’re already building on it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

The transition from a point tool to an operating system is rarely a deliberate procurement decision. It happens quietly through a change in operational direction.

A software tool answers a question a human explicitly asked. Core infrastructure answers questions nobody asked, on an automated schedule, without human intervention. When an account executive opens a research tab at 2 p.m. to look up a prospect, they are using a tool. When an automated routing engine queries the same data layer at 2 a.m. to assign an incoming lead based on parent-subsidiary hierarchy and buying signals, that system is running on an operating system.

The simplest way to determine whether a data source has become your stack’s operating system is to examine your failure modes. If that provider goes dark for a week and a few reps lose a research portal, you are using a tool. But if lead scoring drifts, routing rules misfire and automated workflows stall, your organization is running on infrastructure.

For technical builders evaluating their stack architecture today, the critical challenge is avoiding misclassification. Treating infrastructure like a temporary tool leads to casual vendor swaps that break workflows across your ecosystem. On the flip side, treating a basic tool like infrastructure causes you to overpay for software you could easily swap over a weekend.

To determine what you actually hold, run a simple diagnostic: Price the divorce, not the contract.

Instead of reviewing the renewal invoice, write the actual engineering migration plan required to replace your current data provider. Map every workflow that reads from the layer, every AI agent that pulls its fields into context, every scoring algorithm trained on its records and every downstream system storing copies of its truth. Then, estimate the cost of rewiring those connections in engineering quarters rather than software license dollars.

If replacing the provider means simply swapping user logins, you own a tool. If replacing it requires re-architecting how your systems communicate, you have built an operating system.

When an intelligence layer moves underneath the stack, its core function changes. It stops serving up individual contact lookups to human users and starts performing continuous, unattended background operations.

At the center of that is entity resolution: resolving a CRM record, a web form fill and an attendee on a sales call to the same human and ultimate parent company. It handles corporate hierarchy mapping, ensuring automated agents do not prospect a subsidiary while a strategic enterprise team negotiates with the parent holding company. It constantly maps call transcripts, CRM stage changes and external intent signals onto a single, unified record.

We ran this exact transition internally when I stepped into the CMO seat at ZoomInfo. Rather than making external claims, our first move was instrumenting our own marketing organization directly on our platform — wiring scoring, routing, signal-driven plays and AI workflows into one shared context graph.

The immediate lesson was that an operating system requires uncompromising identity resolution first. Automated workflows built on top of fragmented records or stale lists do not create efficiency; they simply distribute confusion at scale. When an AI agent acts unattended, every field requires clear data provenance, accompanied by strict low-confidence rules: If a record is ambiguous, route it to a human, log the exception, and pause execution.

You can copy a stack in a quarter, but you can’t copy three years of context. The gap between organizations that treat data as a point tool and those that build on an underlying operating system becomes impossible to close quickly.

That compounding advantage manifests across two operational dimensions: velocity from signal to touch and marginal unit economics. When a key champion changes jobs, an agentic workflow wired into an intelligence layer catches the movement, links the executive to historical relationship context and routes a relevant touchpoint the same day. On an operating system, every new workflow you build becomes cheaper than the last because the underlying integration logic already exists.

In an AI-native ecosystem, basic contact records are rapidly commoditizing. Long-term defensibility belongs to the continuous, authoritative data graph underneath — the operating system that every agent and workflow defaults to by design.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

#5504. After topping 2024’s donor list, Elon Musk said he’d do ‘a lot less.’ Since then, he’s given more than George Soros has personally in his lifetime

In May 2025, Elon Musk said he was pulling back from political spending.

“I think in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” Musk said in an interview with Bloomberg at the Qatar Economic Forum. “I think I’ve done enough.”

He then left room to change course: “Well, if I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it,” he said. “I don’t currently see a reason.”

He had just finished the 2024 election cycle as the country’s biggest political donor, according to OpenSecrets. That year, he gave $291.5 million, all to Republicans. The next-largest donor, Timothy Mellon, gave $197 million.

In the 17 months since, Musk has given $427.5 million to federal political committees, according to a Fortune analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 14. That’s nearly $200 million more than George Soros, the man Musk has claimed “astroturfed” anti-Tesla protests. Soros, the Democratic megadonor, has given personally $243.2 million to federal committees in 47 years of FEC records.

Most of Musk’s money arrived after July 1 of this year. SLF PAC, the flagship super PAC for Republican Senate candidates, reported a $75 million check from Musk on Sept. 9 and an $83 million check on Sept. 23. Musk has spent more than $200 million to help elect Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, to the Senate, according to a New York Times analysis.

America PAC, the super PAC Musk funds, reported $165.6 million from him between July 1 and Oct. 14, in its October quarterly and pre-general reports. That includes $8 million in in-kind support from United States of America Inc., one of his companies, which America PAC attributed to Musk.

He also gave $20 million on Sept. 4 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republican candidates. And on Aug. 21, his trust gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton, who is running against Democrat James Talarico.

Other counts put him higher. The Times and OpenSecrets rank Musk as the top donor of the 2026 midterms, at $445.6 million for the full cycle (outside of the FEC, a Fortune analysis of IRS filings found he gave $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association on July 6). The Brennan Center for Justice, which counts his company alongside him, puts the total at $483 million.

Soros’s largest personal checks came before July 2026. He gave Democracy PAC II, one of his family’s two super PACs, $125 million in September 2021 and $50 million in November 2022. In the 2024 cycle, he gave $4.2 million personally to federal committees, FEC records show.

Soros has also given $67.8 million to political groups that report to the IRS, including $24.2 million to Justice & Public Safety PAC, according to IRS filings. FollowTheMoney, which compiles state campaign finance records, lists about $70 million more in state and local contributions. Together, that comes to about $381 million, still less than Musk has given since May 2025.

The comparison changes if groups Soros funds are counted. The Fund for Policy Reform, a nonprofit, has given $210.5 million to Democracy PAC since 2020, including $60 million in January 2024 and $50 million in January 2026, but the nonprofit doesn’t disclose its donors. The Times describes it as a channel for Soros family money and notes that Alex Soros, George’s son, is a director. Counting the fund, Soros’s federal total is $453.7 million, more than Musk has given since his remarks.

The Times counts George and Alex Soros together at $103.4 million this cycle and reports that the family’s two super PACs held about $173 million in cash as of mid-October.

Over his lifetime, Musk has given $723.8 million to federal committees, about three times Soros’s personal federal total, according to Fortune’s analysis of FEC filings. Fortune’s analysis counts contributions each man made to federal political committees as reported to the FEC, including in-kind gifts that recipients attributed to them, and excludes duplicate memo entries. Musk’s totals run through Oct. 14, 2026; Soros’s run through Sept. 9, 2026.

Musk’s totals exclude donations to groups that don’t disclose their donors, as well as any money given after Oct. 14.

#5503. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5502. A Next-Day ‘Thank You’ Can Do More for Your Career Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

Here are three situations when a next-day thank-you can make a meaningful difference.

As a business owner, I often give team members tickets to concerts, theatrical performances or sporting events. Whenever possible, I personalize these gifts. For example, if I know an employee follows a particular sports team, I may offer tickets to see that team play.

Naturally, I appreciate the initial thank you. That acknowledgment usually arrives through our in-office chat tool shortly after the employee receives my offer.

When an employee sends a follow-up text or email after attending the event, especially one that includes a photo or personal detail, it tells me something important about that person’s character.

Employees often share how exciting the final minutes of the game were or mention that the concert exceeded expectations. These details show that the gift was genuinely appreciated.

More importantly, the message demonstrates that the employee doesn’t consider these experiences to be an expected perk of employment. Instead, they recognize that someone made an effort to provide something of value.

When I don’t receive any acknowledgment after the event, I notice. While people sometimes forget or get busy, a consistent lack of expressed appreciation can create an impression of entitlement.  And entitlement is not a quality that encourages employers to invest in someone’s future career development.

Professional favors come in many forms. Your boss might invite you to sit at the company’s table at a major charity event, introduce you to an influential business contact or offer you an opportunity to attend an industry conference.

These gestures deserve more than casual acknowledgment.

Consider the invitation to a charity event. Your first responsibility is to RSVP promptly. RSVP comes from the French phrase Répondez, s’il vous plaît, meaning “Please respond.”

Yet responding to invitations isn’t something everyone does consistently. According to Greenvelope’s RSVP benchmarks, the response rate for conference and meeting invitations is approximately 66%.

Failing to respond promptly can make you appear disorganized or indifferent.

More importantly, recognize the invitation for what it represents: an opportunity to build professional relationships, demonstrate your interpersonal skills and potentially advance your career.

After attending, send a next-day thank-you message. Mention something specific you appreciated, such as an interesting conversation or a valuable introduction.

The same principle applies when a manager recommends you for a special assignment, provides career guidance or makes an introduction that expands your professional network.

Of course, you don’t need to write a formal note every time your boss buys you a cup of coffee. But meaningful favors deserve meaningful appreciation. When you thank someone immediately and follow up afterward, you have taken advantage of demonstrating gratitude twice.

Our SalesFuel research shows that 36% of B2B decision-makers will not do business with a sales professional who demonstrates poor etiquette. Even if you don’t work in sales, that finding should get your attention. Professional behavior influences how others perceive your credibility and character.

Some managers, particularly those from older generations, likely place considerable importance on traditional expressions of courtesy. Don’t miss these opportunities to show your character.

Job candidates typically have three major opportunities to impress prospective employers.

The first comes through their resumes, applications and assessment results. These materials help demonstrate whether candidates possess the skills and abilities required for the position.

The second opportunity occurs during the interview. Candidates can distinguish themselves by discussing their accomplishments, answering questions thoughtfully and communicating their career aspirations.

The third opportunity arrives after the interview ends. A well-written thank-you message sent within 24 hours can reinforce the positive impression you’ve worked hard to establish. This message shouldn’t be a generic, AI-generated paragraph that could be sent to any hiring manager.

Instead, reference something specific from your conversation. Perhaps you appreciated learning about the company’s growth plans or discussing a challenge the team hopes to solve. Briefly reaffirm your interest in the position and explain why the opportunity excites you.

In an age when AI can produce polished resumes and professional correspondence in seconds, genuine personalization matters more than ever. A thoughtful thank you demonstrates communication skills, attention to detail and an understanding of professional etiquette.

It also suggests something employers value: You recognize that another person invested time in considering your future.

A next-day thank-you doesn’t require elaborate language, expensive stationery or a lengthy message. Often, three or four sincere sentences are enough. What matters is the acknowledgment.

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort. You never know which professional relationship may influence your next promotion, assignment or career move.

Gratitude costs very little, but failing to express it can cost you opportunities. Make the next-day thank-you a habit that sets you apart.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

#5501. How Trump’s trade policy is handing Asia to Beijing

Ted Osius is the former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.

For a decade, Washington urged the world’s manufacturers to move their factories out of China and into friendly Southeast Asian states—only to attack the very countries and companies that answered the call.

Usually, U.S. economic statecraft is designed to help American companies succeed abroad. President Donald Trump’s punitive trade program is having the reverse effect. Broad-based import taxes have jolted manufacturers across ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations), including American ones.

Rather than checking China, trade policy is alienating regional partners, harming supply-chain diversification, and eroding America’s influence over the bloc’s trade decisions. The U.S. is engaged in what Evan Feigenbaum, a veteran diplomat and former Republican, terms a “reverse pivot.” Bogged down in foreign crises elsewhere, Washington now projects hesitation and retreat in Asia rather than dynamic leadership.

In the months after President Trump’s April 2025 announcement of “Liberation Day” tariffs, some of ASEAN’s non-tariff barriers fell. A few countries used the exogenous threat to bring about needed reforms.  Deals were done, including Boeing sales and–at least prospective–LNG contracts. It appeared that coercion worked, at least in the short term. In February the Supreme Court struck down much of the initial tariff regime and the administration pivoted to workarounds: 150-day emergency measures under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, and expansive Section 301 investigations into forced labor, intellectual property violations, and “excess capacity.”

America’s labor, intellectual property, and excess-capacity concerns are really about China, not Southeast Asia. The administration substituted an improvised China policy for a coherent Southeast Asia policy—a strategic blunder. By treating regional partners as collateral damage to show that China isn’t singled out, Washington is undercutting its most reliable partners and allies.

Nowhere is the absurdity of this approach more evident than in the supply chains themselves. For nearly a decade, multinational corporations have redirected capital and manufacturing from China into Vietnam, Malaysia, India, and the Philippines. The goal of these “China plus one” strategies was to insulate critical industries from geopolitical risk and move them into friendly states.

Washington’s tariff regime now undercuts this strategy. Southeast Asian export hubs suffer far more than the United States when Chinese firms attempt illicit transshipment, while subsidized Chinese overcapacity squeezes local producers. The broader reality, though, is not widespread evasion but deep and legitimate supply-chain integration. By imposing blanket punitive duties, Washington is tightening the vise on the very partners helping achieve that diversification.

As Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, has observed, Washington created the incentive structure for alternate supply routes and is now penalizing regional partners for using them.

These tariffs aren’t even achieving Trump’s stated goals. Higher costs and a shortage of skilled domestic labor mean production lines won’t magically shift to U.S. shores. Bilateral trade deficits with Southeast Asian economies remain largely unchanged; regional exporters, U.S. importers, and consumers are simply absorbing higher costs.

ASEAN nations have long been masters of dynamic hedging—exemplified by Vietnam’s “bamboo diplomacy”—balancing China against the United States. None of them want to be dominated by Beijing, making Washington their natural partner. Yet as U.S. policy grows increasingly erratic and punitive, it inadvertently pushes them to hedge elsewhere.

As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, the weaponization of economic tools forces middle powers to organize: “If we are not at the table, we are on the menu.”

Coercive tactics failed with Canada, and they will fail in Asia. Recently, politically appointed U.S. ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha told local and international business leaders that he received orders from the President to “bring home the money,” so they needed to double their U.S. investments.  The demand went over like a lead balloon. Capital flows are not surging into the United States; they are pivoting further into Asia.

This friction runs counter to decades of bipartisan precedent. Since the 1985 Plaza Accord, which catalyzed an era of industrial integration in Southeast Asia, American leaders have recognized that regional partners thrive under predictable, rules-based frameworks rather than blunt coercion. Today’s transactional posture risks creating a durable trust deficit that will penalize American enterprise for a generation.

Since America pulled out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership in favor of country-by-country negotiations, its absence at the table has been filled by others. ASEAN is now building institutional networks that bypass Washington altogether. Member states are working with accords like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

American companies have not forgotten the benefits of clear rules of the road in a multilateral context. They have worked closely with ASEAN negotiators toward the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). Spanning 11 nations, nearly 700 million consumers, and an estimated $2 trillion digital marketplace, DEFA would establish comprehensive standards for cross-border data governance, cybersecurity, digital identity, and artificial intelligence.

As Washington retreats behind tariffs and procedural disputes, Southeast Asia—with input from U.S. companies—is writing the regulatory architecture of the 21st-century digital economy.

Washington builds walls while ASEAN builds architecture.

Southeast Asia does not wish to decouple from the United States. Four ASEAN nations—Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore—rank among America’s top 20 bilateral trading partners. Private enterprise, investment flows, and educational links remain extraordinarily resilient.

But in statecraft, trust is the ultimate currency. U.S. influence in the Indo-Pacific was never sustained through sheer market size or coercive leverage alone; it thrived because Washington offered an institutional vision grounded in mutual benefit and reliable rules. If Washington continues to treat its Asian partners as transactional pawns in a zero-sum struggle with Beijing, it will discover they have other trading partners. America risks economic isolation and strategic diminishment in the century of the Pacific Rim.

#5499. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5498. Apple outpaces sales expectations as it continues to battle surging memory chip costs

Apple beat its quarterly financial expectations in Chief Executive John Ternus’s first earnings report since taking over Tim Cook’s post in September, though the company continues to be pressured by a surge in memory chip costs.

The iPhone maker posted revenue of $114.5 billion in its fiscal fourth-quarter, up 12% year-over-year and above Wall Street targets of $113.4 billion. Its profit was $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per share.

Ternus extolled the company’s expanding lineup of products during a conference call with analysts, including the all-important iPhone business, which grew 17%, to $57.58 billion, in the three months ending on Sept. 26.

Apple said that it expects overall revenue to grow between 7% and 10% year-over-year in the current, holiday quarter, seasonally Apple’s strongest quarter of the year. The forecast suggests a range of $153.8 billion to $158.2 billion, compared to the $153.2 billion that analysts were expecting. But the outlook for profit margins seems to have left investors cold.

Shares of the $4.9 trillion company fell as much as 4% in after hours trading on Monday, before recovering some ground to trade down 2.7%.

Many investors have been watching the impact of rising memory chip prices on Apple and how it will weigh on profit margins. To help offset what Ternus described on Monday’s call as an “unprecedented” situation in the memory market, Apple has raised prices across its product line. Apple’s gross margin weighed in at 47.9% in the recently ended quarter, landing near the high end of its forecast range and above the 47.2% gross margin it posted in the year-ago period. But Apple’s chief financial officer, Kevan Parekh, said tariff refunds lifted the gross margin by roughly one percentage point; without them, it would have been lower.

For the current, holiday quarter, Apple said it expects gross margins to decline, ranging between 45% and 46% due to rising memory costs and some costs associated with ramping up its Siri AI service.

Ternus has marked his first couple of months at Apple with a slew of product releases that have helped the engineer savant show off Apple’s latest innovations and ease into the new job. That has included the September launch of the foldable iPhone Duo, followed by new home products, and last week’s unveiling of Apple’s first touch screen MacBook Pro.

Ternus said in a written statement that iPhone revenue reached a September quarter record and Services posted an all-time high, “capping off our best fiscal year ever.”

“We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” he said. “Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.”

Apple’s Services revenue, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, was $31.57 billion, up roughly 10% year-over-year. But sales in the company’s iPad business and its wearables business both declined.

Apple’s earnings followed financial reports from its Big Tech peers. Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon all revealed their latest earnings in the last two weeks. While the companies generally had positive results, shares in the Nasdaq Composite have sunk in recent days as investors have weighed Big Tech’s positive growth, especially in cloud-computing demand for AI services, against the hundreds of billions Microsoft, Amazon, and others are spending in AI infrastructure.
